1127-othello:
Othello, a Moorish general in Venice's service, marries Desdemona in secret, and his ensign Iago, passed over for promotion, plots his ruin with lies about Desdemona and the young Cassio. William Shakespeare's tragedy follows Othello from love and trust to jealous rage and murder in Cyprus.

Iago, the most coldly brilliant villain in Shakespeare, works by hints and half-truths, and Othello's fall still shocks. Desdemona's innocence and Emilia's late courage frame the horror. The tragedy stands as a study of jealousy, race, and trust destroyed, and it grips every audience.
11680-george-eliot-a-critical-study-of-h:
George Willis Cooke's 1884 critical study takes up George Eliot's life, writings, and philosophy together. A preface to the second edition corrects an essay on lady novelists, first credited to Eliot, now known as George Henry Lewes's work, though its opinions match Eliot's own.

Chapters cover early life, work as translator and editor, and marriage, with later pages on Lewes's books on Spanish drama and Goethe. A passage on home scenes, with oaks, star-flowers, and speedwell, shows Cooke's claim that familiar fields are the mother tongue of imagination. The study is a Victorian appraisal, not a life alone.
12631-the-seven-little-sisters-who-live-:
Jane Andrews's Seven Little Sisters Who Live on the Round Ball That Floats in the Air, introduced by Louisa Parsons Hopkins, tells geography through seven girls around the world. A memorial of Andrews, born 1833 and died 1887, opens the book, followed by the ball itself, the little brown baby, Agoonack the Esquimau sister and how she lives through long summer.

Gemila, child of the desert, a little mountain maiden, Pen-Se, a little dark girl, Louise of the Rhine and Louise of the western forest complete the sisters. Andrews writes for three little friends, Marnie, Bell and Geordie, in simple, affectionate prose. The book is a classic children's geography, teaching the earth through imagined sisters.
12641-the-queen-of-the-air-being-a-study:
John Ruskin's Queen of the Air, a study of Greek myths of cloud and storm, grows from a lecture given partly at University College, London, on 9 March 1869. Athena Chalinitis, Athena in the heavens and Athena the Restrainer, who helped Bellerophon bridle Pegasus the flying cloud, fronts the book.

Ruskin asks permission to approach mythology in a temper unlike common treatment. He admits that we, like the Greeks, may err in faith, and that others' convictions, however singular, may hold truth where our own, however reasonable, may fail. Cloud, storm, Athena and nature symbolism follow. The book offers Ruskin at his most poetic and moral, reading myth as natural theology.
12819-dick-prescott-s-second-year-at-wes:
Dick Prescott's second year at West Point brings hazing lectures, Flirtation Walk, and a court-martial that tests his friends. Greg Holmes debates girls and mischief, while Cadet Dodge hears things he should not, and a false charge puts Dick under close arrest. A fight in the barracks and a riding drill discovery turn the tide.

Through it all Dick learns the soldier's glory is not parade shine but standing true when accused. Summer camp, visitors from home, and pitching for the Army nine lighten the strain. Hancock's tale mixes academy detail with a clean story of loyalty and honour.
13237-strange-visitors-a-series-of-origi:
Published in 1871, Strange Visitors claims to give papers by spirits of Irving, Willis, Thackeray, Brontë, Richter, Byron, Humboldt, Hawthorne, Wesley, and Browning, dictated through a clairvoyant in trance. Contents run from Margaret Fuller on literature in spirit life to Byron to his accusers, Hawthorne on apparitions, and Poe on the lost soul. The book is a spiritualist curiosity of its age.

One paper says Napoleon fell when he tore the magnetic filaments binding him to Josephine, like a wreck on St. Helena's shore. Another holds that each planet has a spirit world, with magnetic rays exchanging thoughts between earth and spirit globe. The papers mix philosophy, satire, and prophecy, and they show how Victorian readers sought voices from beyond.
1362-tom-swift-and-his-undersea-search-o:
Victor Appleton sends Tom Swift beneath the waves in a submarine of his own design, hunting a sunken treasure on the floor of the Atlantic. The tale moves through deep-sea wonders, rival salvors, and a wreck that guards its gold with storms and sharks.

Tom's inventions and his pluck carry the adventure, with his friends at his side. The book mixes science fiction with treasure-hunt thrills. It suits young readers who like Swift's formula of brains, machines, and danger under the sea. Swift's undersea hunt mixes science fiction with treasure thrills.
15602-statistical-historical-and-politic:
William Charles Wentworth, a native of the colony, published this statistical, historical, and political description of New South Wales in London in 1819, with Whittaker. Its subtitle promises an enumeration of advantages these colonies offer for emigration. It claims their superiority in many respects over those possessed by the United States. Four parts and an appendix carry the argument.

Part one gives a statistical account of settlements in New Holland. It opens with New South Wales on the eastern coast. That colony was first found by the Dutch in 1616, lying between nine and thirty-nine degrees south. Later parts judge fifteen years of government, suggest changes in policy, and propose changes in the system of rule. Wentworth writes as a colonial advocate, eager to draw settlers and reform, and the book is a founding document of Australian self-description.
16909-the-halo:
Bettina von Hutten wrote this 1907 novel, issued by Dodd, Mead in New York with a frontispiece by B. Martin Justice and a dedication to a dear lost friend. A prologue opens on a dusty Norman road, where an old blind man plays a cracked fiddle under apple trees, grinning as it shrieks, with a yellow dog beside him. No other living thing is in sight.

Von Hutten builds a tale of love, loss, and a halo of grace around flawed folk, in the high romantic style of her day. The Norman road and its fiddler set a mood of sorrow and wonder. Readers who like old romantic novels will find strong feeling, vivid scenes, and a story that asks what light can survive in broken lives.
20067-zun-i-fetiches-second-annual-repor:
Zuñi Fetiches appeared in the second annual report of the Bureau of Ethnology. It studies sacred objects used by the Zuñi people of the Southwest. The text explains how people may give a thing in nature a life like their own. A force in nature can seem to act like an animal or a person.

Such reports were early United States attempts to record Native belief with care. The study names forms, uses, and beliefs tied to each fetish. Readers get a close, dated record of Zuñi faith as outsiders then saw it. It still serves those who study how such records were made.
20419-gigolo:
Gigolo tells a story of city nightlife, where dancers and hangers-on drift through clubs and dance halls. One woman keeps coming back despite repeated rebuffs. She leaves her name at the desk, hoping for word of the elusive Nick.

Smitty, Mike, or Elmer might bandy her name about, but she seems to lack the pride to stay away. The tale watches her hope against the cold rules of that world. It gives a sharp, unsentimental picture of the dance-hall scene and the people who lived for its lights and music.
2058-messer-marco-polo:
Brian Oswald Donn-Byrne, known as Donn Byrne, retells the life of Marco Polo as a romance. It follows the Venetian merchant from his youth to the court of Kublai Khan and his long road home. The author note stresses Byrne's Irish feeling. Donn-Byrne, born in New York and raised in Ireland, brought a Celtic lilt to his tales.

Byrne writes in a lyrical, old-world style, full of colour and adventure, and the book suits readers who like their history told as story. Marco's travels, wonders, and return give the novel its shape and its charm. His Marco Polo blends history with romance, so the traveller's marvels read like a storyteller's art.
20611-mr-grex-of-monte-carlo:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's Mr. Grex of Monte Carlo is a thriller of intrigue on the Riviera. Its hero looks in on a scene of casino splendor. After the first few moments of careless interest, his eyes undergo a curious change at what he sees.

He is contemplating one of the sights of the world: the gaming rooms of Monte Carlo in full blaze. Behind that glitter, the plot runs on spies, stolen plans, and disguised identities. Oppenheim wrote dozens of such tales, and this one shows his formula at its smoothest: bright rooms, dark purposes, and a gentleman in danger.
2267-othello:
Othello, a Moorish general in Venetian service, marries Desdemona in secret, and his ensign Iago sets out to destroy him. Othello moves from Cyprus's wars to a bedroom murder, as Iago plants a handkerchief and whispers doubts until jealousy unhinges a noble mind. Shakespeare makes the villain his most candid character, confiding his plans straight to the audience.

Desdemona's innocence and Emilia's late truth-telling sharpen the horror of the close. The play probes race, trust, and the ease with which love curdles into suspicion. It stands as one of the most painful tragedies ever staged.
23451-little-yellow-wang-lo:
M. C. Bell wrote this Dumpy Book for Children, number twenty six in the series, about Little Yellow Wang Lo, a boy who lives on a houseboat and tends ducks. Each morning he rises early, calls the ducks round the boat, feeds them, and watches them swim down river for fishes and frogs until supper time.

One hot day, Fo Pa, a very fat little man, sends him ashore in his Sunday clothes to sell the ducks at market and buy a pig for roasting. Wang Lo's eyes shine at the trip and at the thought of roast pork, and he rows off in haste, selling all his fat ducks in one market corner. The tale, with bright pictures, gives small children a warm glimpse of river life, work, and a boy's proud errand.
23889-charley-de-milo:
Larry M. Harris wrote Charley de Milo, a science fiction story set amid a carnival midway. Rockets climb, and Professor Lightning seems not to care. Outside talkers bark for grind shows, rides, and spectacles. Hell Drivers, the biggest auto show in fifty states, and dances learned at the court of the Sultan all cost the fourth part of a dollar bill.

The story's teasing premise is stated up front: a man might actually be held back by possessing two sound, working arms. With Hamlet's To be, or not to be as epigraph, Harris builds a midway tale around that odd idea. Kewpie dolls, Hawaiian leis, and a life-size model of Luna in three dimensions fill the midway.
28022-el-diablo:
Brayton Norton wrote El Diablo, illustrated by Dan Sayre Groesbeck and published in Indianapolis by Bobbs-Merrill in 1921, after copyright by Sunset Magazine. The novel opens with Richard Gregory waking fully dressed in thick grey fog, taking his automatic and rifle as a hand touches his shoulder.

Thirty-two chapters follow forbidden waters, jetsam, tangled threads, salvage, a strike, a battle at Northwest Harbor, and a fight in a cave, with the island's prisoner and the fangs of Mascola. Norton writes sea adventure with mystery and romance, in the popular magazine manner of the 1920s.
29557-the-lord-of-glory-meditations-on-t:
A. C. Gaebelein gathered these meditations on the person, work, and glory of Jesus Christ from the first pages of Our Hope magazine, where brief meditations had run for years. Copyrighted in 1910, the book was printed by the magazine's publication office in New York, with Pickering and Inglis of Glasgow and Toronto. Friends had urged that the notes be issued in book form so blessed truths might be preserved more permanently.

Gaebelein gives three reasons for the series. Christ is worthy of all honor and the first place in all things. His people need his person, past and present work, power, glory, and future manifestation kept before them. The meditations are short, devout, and plain. Readers of devotional literature will find a warm, earnest companion for daily reading.
30494-the-adventures-of-a-brownie-as-tol:
Miss Mulock tells The Adventures of a Brownie as told to her child, illustrated and copyrighted in 1908 by McLoughlin Brothers of New York. Six adventures follow Brownie with the cook, with the cherry tree, in the farmyard, on a ride, on the ice, and with the clothes.

Poems follow, including The Blackbird and the Rooks, The Shaking of the Pear-Tree, The Wonderful Apple-Tree, The Jealous Boy, The Story of the Birkenhead, Birds in the Snow, and The Little Comforter. Later verses add Don't Be Afraid, Girl and Boy, Agnes at Prayer, Going to Work, and Three Companions. Mulock blends fairy mischief with gentle verse for young children.
31273-the-arawack-language-of-guiana-in-:
D. G. Brinton's 1871 study, printed in Philadelphia, examines the Arawack language of Guiana in its linguistic and ethnological relations. The Arawacks, about two thousand souls living in British and Dutch Guiana between the Corentyn and Pomeroon rivers, call themselves lukkunu, men. Neighbors apply the contemptuous aruac, meal-eaters, for their diet of Mauritia palm pith and cassava root.

Brinton argues they once occupied the whole West Indian archipelago nearly to the northern continent. Whether their affiliations lie with northern or southern mainland tribes decides the course of primitive migration in the western world. He links them to the people Columbus and Peter Martyr described. The book is a foundational work of South American linguistics and ethnology.
32290-a-letter-to-a-gentleman-in-the-cou:
A Letter to a Gentleman in the Country, from His Friend in London, printed for and sold by J. Lacy in London in 1757 at one shilling, gives an authentic and circumstantial account of Admiral Byng. It covers his confinement, behaviour, and death, as attested by the gentlemen who were present. Its motto, Mens conscia Recti, a mind conscious of right, frames the account. The letter form promises an insider's report, not a historian's summary.

Lacy advertises companion pamphlets on the same case. They include Further Particulars from original papers by a gentleman of Oxford, and a collection of suppressed letters and detached pieces. A further address offers genuine copies of letters between Byng and the Secretary of the Admiralty. Readers get a contemporary pamphlet on one of the century's most debated executions, told by witnesses and sold while the controversy was fresh.
32762-michelangelo:
Romain Rolland tells the life of Michelangelo, translated by Frederick Street and published by Duffield and Company in 1921. Born at Caprese on March 6, 1475, Michelangelo grew from childhood and youth into the sculptor and painter of the Sistine ceiling, the David, the Pieta, and the tomb of Julius II.

Six chapters follow his work under Julius II, the failure of his great plans, his friendship with Vittoria Colonna, and his old age and death in 1564. Rolland closes by judging his genius and his grip on Italian art, arguing that later masters reflected their century while Michelangelo towered over it. Illustrations and a catalogue of works complete the volume.
36930-murillo:
Murillo is an art book in the Masterpieces in Colour series, edited by T Leman Hare. It covers the Spanish painter Murillo, whose dates are given as sixteen eighteen to sixteen eighty two. Colour plates lead the book, starting with the Immaculate Conception from the Louvre as frontispiece. The text calls that canvas greatly admired and skilfully composed.

More than a dozen pictures of that subject by Murillo are undisputed, the opening notes. Many other copies and imitations in his manner are on offer in Spain, it warns. Plate by plate, the book teaches readers to know the true master's soft saints and cherubs. Cheap colour printing brought gallery art to home readers in this series.
36989-some-phases-of-sexual-morality-and:
Charles Francis Adams read this paper to the Massachusetts Historical Society in June 1891. John Wilson printed it at Cambridge the same year, drawn from the society's record. Its theme is morals and church rule in colonial New England.

Adams had dug deep in the records of old Braintree, now Quincy, for a town history in 1883. Letters, journals, and oral tales came into his hands for that work. They bore on social customs and on church and state in the Puritan age. The study of them led him to this frank paper. Church discipline for sins of the flesh, told from the records themselves, shows a side of the founders rarely shown in school books.
37004-three-accounts-of-peterloo-by-eyew:
Three Accounts of Peterloo was published at Manchester in 1921. The university press issued it in a historical series. Bruton, of Manchester Grammar School, edited the texts. Three eyewitnesses give the accounts. Bishop Stanley tells what he saw, and his trial evidence of 1822 is added. Lord Hylton, then a young lieutenant named Jolliffe, writes the second. John Benjamin Smith, a Manchester man, writes the third. Portraits of Stanley and Smith face the pages. Two plans of the field are printed for the reader. Appendices treat the relics of the day. A banner, constables' staves, and a hussar's plume are listed.

Bamford's cottage at Middleton is pictured among them. Notes weigh the casualties and the women and children present. The volume is a school of evidence on one famous hour.
37489-an-historical-narrative-of-the-gre:
Gideon Harvey wrote this Historical Narrative of the Great and Terrible Fire of London. The pamphlet first appeared in 1769, a century after the fire. This text comes from an 1855 reprint in a volume of Daniel Defoe's works. There it sat beside Defoe's Journal of the Plague Year.

The narrative opens as Londoners return after the plague abates. On September 2, 1666, fire breaks out at a baker's shop in Pudding Lane. Rotten wooden houses and stores of goods feed the flames. Billingsgate ward is ashes within hours. The fire rushes downhill to the bridge and takes Saint Magnus church. Checked at the bridge, it marches back through the city. Harvey writes as if the fire were a conquering army.
37591-chance-in-chains-a-story-of-monte-:
Guy Thorne wrote Chance in Chains, a story of Monte Carlo, published at New York in 1914. Thorne had written When It Was Dark and The Drunkard. A front plate shows Basil Gregory before a pile of gold.

Chapter one opens far from the tables, in the Mont Parnasse power station at Paris at nine at night. Thirty dynamos of the Société Générale Electrique light half of eastern Paris. Workmen in blue blouses tend the whirring copper drums under arc lamps. The superintendent watches from a glass room of white tiles. Thorne builds the scene slowly before the story of chance begins.
39353-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Cambridge issued the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica in 1910 and 1911, a summit of print reference. The stretch gathered here runs from Hero to Hindu Chronology in one thick slice of the alphabet. Hero the engineer of Alexandria leads it off.

Short lives crowd the H's: Herwegh the German poet stands among them. Hesse-Cassel, the old German state, takes a long entry of its own. The editors of this plain text note how signs and accents were handled, and list small printer's faults they fixed. Subscripts, Greek letters, and roots get plain marks in place of fine type. What the slice keeps is the meat: signed articles, dense with fact, from one of the last great one-set sums of all knowledge.
41290-arbuthnotiana-the-story-of-the-st-:
Arbuthnotiana, issued by the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library at Los Angeles in 1972 as publication 154 of the Augustan Reprint Society, reprints two pieces. The first is The Story of the St Alb-ns Ghost, of 1712; the second is a catalogue of Doctor Arbuthnot's library, of 1779. Patricia Köster introduces the volume.

Her introduction compares the editions of the Story. The second edition makes three small changes from the first, and the third and fourth seem line-for-line reprints of the second. In the fifth, somebody altered the typography of past verb forms, dropping apostrophes, perhaps under the spur of Swift's Proposal for the English tongue, printed a week after the fourth edition.
42620-prefaces-to-four-seventeenth-centu:
Prefaces to Four Seventeenth Century Romances holds four old front essays. A Clark library set reprinted the rare texts in nineteen fifty three. Charles Davies wrote the lead in for the four short works. Each front essay fronts a romance of the sixteen hundreds in its first print.

Roger Boyle pleads his case for his own long prose tale of love. George Mackenzie writes a full plea in defence of romances as a kind. Two more kin hands, one a great man of science, add their pleas. The set shows how new prose tales won a place by bold first words. Scholars of prose roots form the prime readership of the small book.
44078-the-trail-boys-of-the-plains-or-th:
The Trail Boys of the Plains, or The Hunt for the Big Buffalo, by Jay Winthrop Allen, was published by George Sully and Company at New York, copyright 1915. Walter S Rogers illustrated the hunt. Chet Havens braids a whiplash as the story opens, asking whether such a buffalo really exists.

His chum Dig Fordham, carving his initials with a dull jackknife, dreams of going out after the herd and capturing the king of them all. The chapters promise bears' dens, an old tunnel, dog soldiers, a wolf ring, and royal game before the hunt ends.
44351-agent-nine-solves-his-first-case-a:
Graham Dean wrote Agent Nine Solves His First Case, a story of the daring exploits of the G Men, copyrighted at Chicago in 1935. Thirty-two chapters carry the tale. A surprise call opens it, then an empty room and Bob has a visitor. The door moves, a sliver of steel, and in the darkened room follow. Sirens in the night, the paper vanishes, and suspicions fill the next heads.

On the ledge, strained tempers, steps in the hall, and Bob fights back lead to special agent nine. The radio secret, meagre hopes, and the missing paper fill the middle. Shots in the night, the lone fight, anxious hours, and the first clue lead on. The chase ends, and the last head is federal agent. The first chapter sets Bob Houston, a young clerk in the records office of the War Department, walking back to the office through chill fall rain.
44458-tools-and-materials-illustrating-t:
Tools and Materials Illustrating the Japanese Method of Colour Printing is a museum catalogue by Edward Strange, issued at London in 1913. It describes a collection shown at the Victoria and Albert Museum. The front picture shows the making of colour prints in Japan, after a famed print in the museum's own holdings. Women are shown carving the wood blocks in that image.

The contents move through a short history, then the drawing, the cutting of the block, and the printing itself. Paper gets its own section, and books of reference close the list. A prefatory note says the pamphlet was made for use with the shown collection. That collection of tools, materials, and examples was brought together on purpose. It lets a visitor follow a print from first sketch to finished sheet.
4694-mademoiselle-of-monte-carlo:
William Le Queux published Mademoiselle of Monte Carlo in 1921, opening at a roulette table in Monte Carlo. A tall, good-looking young Englishman whispers to an older friend that the handsome woman winning at the table is the same woman he knows. He fears she might recognise him, and he longs to make her disclose what she knows about his poor father's mysterious end.

His friend doubts she ever will, given what is said about the Mademoiselle of Monte Carlo. From that first chapter, called The Suicide's Chair, Le Queux builds a thriller of gambling, secrets, and revenge on the Riviera. Readers get a fast, melodramatic mystery, with casinos, disguises, and a father's death to avenge, in the popular style of its day.
47883-birds-and-nature-vol-12-no-3-augus:
Birds and Nature, volume twelve number three, is the October 1902 number of a magazine illustrated by colour photography. A poem by William Cullen Bryant, Autumn Woods, opens the issue. Short pieces of verse break up the natural history.

The Philippine Sun-Bird leads the articles: sun-birds, the text says, hold the place in the eastern tropics that humming birds hold in the west. More than one hundred species wear bright plumage and feed at flowers. The Great Gray Owl, the green-crested flycatcher, and the Louisiana water-thrush follow. The leaf butterfly, some snails of the ocean, and the tomato fill later pages.
47952-birds-and-all-nature-vol-5-no-5-ma:
Birds and All Nature, in its May 1899 number, is a Chicago nature magazine. The Nature Study Publishing Company issued it, with colour photographs as pictures. The number closes the magazine's fifth volume. Its contents mix birds, beasts, plants, and short verses for nature lovers.

The cedar waxwing leads the number, drawn five-sevenths of life size. Lynds Jones praises its silky plumage and courtly bearing in his sketch. The preacher-bird, Bonaparte's gull, and the water thrush follow among the birds. Coffee earns two separate pieces in one issue, a sign of its wide interest. The cony, the baboon, and the tarsier represent the animal kingdom in turn. A defence of some birds and a crusade for feathers plead the birds' own cause.
48466-birds-and-all-nature-vol-7-no-5-ma:
Birds and All Nature for May 1900 is volume seven, number five of a magazine shown by color photography. The contents mix verse and short nature pieces. A poem to May opens the number, signed with two initials. Then comes a verse piece on hearing the bird sing, by Nelly Hart Woodworth. Uncle Nick on fishing, the magpie, and a butterfly's history follow.

The dead bird, the field daisy, and a sunken forest stand among the short pieces. The red-breasted nuthatch, wandering birds, and the purple martin are treated in turn. Johnny Appleseed, the ring-necked dove, and the opossum appear in the list. Pieces on dogs, easy lessons in evolution, and the cecropia moth follow. Where vegetables came from, birds and farmers, thyme, the raven, and the wild flowers of May close the contents. An index to the volume and a general index end the number.
4924-dry-farming-a-system-of-agriculture:
Dry farming, as this manual explains it, means growing useful crops without irrigation on land receiving twenty inches of rain a year or less. In districts of torrential rain, high wind, or badly timed rainfall, the same methods apply up to twenty-five or even thirty inches, since water is lost faster than it falls.

The book sets out how to keep moisture in the soil, choose crops suited to dry country, and farm profitably where irrigation cannot reach. No author appears in the catalog record, but the system is laid out plainly for working farmers. Readers in arid regions get a practical guide to an agriculture built around saving every drop of rain.
50102-the-river-motor-boat-boys-on-the-a:
Harry Gordon wrote this boys' adventure, copyrighted in 1913, one of his River Motor Boat Boys books. The frontispiece shows Frank's searchlight catching an Indian with a knife in hand, ready to spring.

The contents open with all ready for the Amazon, a call from the darkness, and a brown leather bag. Two guests and an arrest follow, then a boy from Peru and a five hundred dollar reward at Para. Later chapters bring a campfire in the jungle, a plot against the Rambler, and a battle for the boat. The secret of Cloud Island waits near the end. The opening scene is a rainy night aboard, with Jule missing from his guard post. Boys get river adventure at full throttle.
50503-forty-eighth-annual-report-of-the-:
The Forty Eighth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology covers the fiscal year 1930 to 1931. The Government Printing Office printed it at Washington in 1933 for the Smithsonian Institution. It sold for two dollars. M W Stirling, the chief, sent it to Dr C G Abbot, secretary of the Smithsonian, on July 15, 1931.

The report of the chief treats systematic researches, special researches, and editorial work and publications. The distribution of publications, the library, the collections, and property follow. An accompanying paper holds a general index to the annual reports of the bureau, volumes one to forty eight. The bureau work ran to the study of native peoples and Hawaiians and the digging and keeping of ancient remains under Smithsonian direction. Scholars get the year work of the nation Indian bureau in one volume.
54622-reports-relating-to-the-sanitary-c:
Reports Relating to the Sanitary Condition of the City of London is by John Simon, surgeon to St Thomas's Hospital and officer of health to the City. John W Parker and Son published the reports at London in 1854. Simon dedicates the reprint to his father, Louis Michael Simon of the Stock Exchange.

The reports were addressed to the Commissioners of Sewers and first printed only for the Corporation's use. This volume gathers the first five annual reports, with further remarks on water-supply. An appendix of tables illustrates the sanitary condition of the City. Reports on City burial-grounds and on extramural interments close the book. Simon writes that the reports represent years of anxious labour, offered as a record of endeavours to do his duty.
55526-the-law-of-the-bolo:
Stanley Portal Hyatt wrote The Law of the Bolo, a novel of the Philippines printed at Boston. Twelve chapters carry motto like heads, each starting 'How.' The bolo is the long knife of the islands, and its law rules the hills.

Felizardo, a wizened peasant of sixty, had lived quietly near Manila, fishing and working his hemp patch. Love for Dolores Lasara, a teniente's daughter, changed him. When the Americans replaced the Spaniards, his path crossed officers, commissioners, and gallows builders. Hyatt tells how Felizardo took to the hills and how he at last made peace.
58570-condition-of-the-american-colored-:
Condition of the American Colored Population, and of the Colony at Liberia is a pamphlet issued in Boston in 1833, presenting facts gathered from official documents and correspondence. Its first subject is the enslaved population of the United States: their numbers and increase, their civil disabilities, and their intellectual and moral condition. A second part reports on the colony at Liberia, founded for free Black emigrants.

The opening table compares the censuses of 1820 and 1830 state by state. It shows slavery shrinking in the North. Meanwhile the enslaved grew by tens of thousands in Virginia and the South. Maryland and the District of Columbia actually declined. The pamphlet uses such figures to argue about the measures proposed for relief, weighing gradual change at home against the Liberian colony abroad.
60011-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Widger made an index of the Gutenberg works of Maturin Murray Ballou. The index lists each work with its own full part list. The Sea-Witch leads the roll of Ballou's long tale shelf. The Circassian Slave and The Duke's Prize stand in that roll. The Heart's Secret and Foot-Prints of Travel share the list.

Due West, a History of Cuba, and Malta's tale fill the mid. The Southern Cross and a life of Hosea Ballou stand there. Equatorial America and Fanny Campbell close the tale row. Pearls of Thought adds a book of brief wise lines at the end. Each work's parts are set out so guests can find their place. Fans of dime tales get a key.
62338-the-countess-of-rudolstadt-a-seque:
The Countess of Rudolstadt, a sequel to Consuelo, is a novel by George Sand, translated from the French by Fayette Robinson. This English edition came from Walter Scott in London. The story opens at the Italian opera house in Berlin, built for a king who filled the pit with soldiers. Consuelo, the great singer of the earlier novel, now moves through courts and conspiracies.

Across forty-one chapters and an epilogue, Sand weaves music, secret societies, and revolution into one vast romance. Prussian militarism, booed or applauded on orders, stands against the free life of art. The novel is among Sand's most ambitious, joining her love of music to her faith in human progress. Robinson's translation carried it to English readers in cheap, portable form.
63087-color-standards-and-color-nomencla:
Color Standards and Color Nomenclature is a work by Robert Ridgway, curator of the division of birds at the United States National Museum. It came out at Washington in 1912, published by the author. The book holds fifty-three colored plates and eleven hundred and fifteen named colors. A color wheel stands at its front.

The book is given to Jose C. Zeledon of San Jose, Costa Rica. The dedication calls him a true and firm friend of more than forty years. He was host, guide, and companion on trips among the rich forests, grand mountains, and fair plains of his own land, it says. His backing made the end of the work in hand— as the text breaks off. The book is a standard list of colors and their names, made for men of science and art.
65027-a-narrative-of-some-remarkable-inc:
Solomon Bayley, formerly a slave in the state of Delaware, wrote this narrative of remarkable incidents in his own life. Harvey and Darton and others printed it at London in 1825, and it was published for his benefit. A few remarks by Robert Hurnard stand before it, with a motto from Second Corinthians: persecuted, but not forsaken.

Hurnard met the account of Bayley's escape from slavery in America in 1820 and inquired into the man at Wilmington. Bayley had learned the cooper's trade, then gave it up from scruples, believing barrels helped the sale of ardent spirits, and took to farm labour. Meeting the governor of Delaware, he spoke to him of the responsibility of his station, and was rewarded with the oversight of one of the governor's farms, sharing the profits. Hurnard vouches for Bayley's character from many respectable inhabitants of Wilmington.
67629-an-illustrated-dictionary-of-words:
Illustrated Dictionary of Words Used in Art and Archaeology is a reference book. Mollett compiled it, printed at London in the year 1883. Sampson Low issued it from Crown Buildings on Fleet Street. Mollett had written lives of Rembrandt and of Wilkie for a series. A front plate shows the apse of St Paul Without the Walls.

Terms cover architecture, arms, bronzes, Christian art, and colour in turn. Costume, decoration, devices, emblems, and heraldry fill the alphabet onward. Lace, personal ornaments, pottery, painting, and sculpture close the scope list. Each term comes with its derivation traced for the student reader. The work began as an amended edition of Bosc of Paris.
68234-martha-schofield-pioneer-negro-edu:
Matilda Evans wrote Martha Schofield, Pioneer Negro Educator, copyrighted in 1916 and printed in Columbia, South Carolina. Evans, a doctor, was herself a graduate of the Schofield School. The book joins a life of the teacher with a historical and philosophical review of the Reconstruction period in South Carolina.

Evans dedicates the work to the men and women who braved danger and social scorn to educate a lowly race. The opening chapter, called The Hunted Beast, tells of Laura Duncan, an escaped slave who fled bloodhounds into the Schofield home at Darby, Pennsylvania, about 1857. Martha Schofield, a Quaker, later carried schooling to freed people in the South. The book preserves both her story and the hard world in which she worked.
68549-the-poisoned-paradise-a-romance-of:
Robert Service spins a Riviera tale in The Poisoned Paradise, a romance of Monte Carlo, printed in New York in 1922. Dodd Mead made the book, with three printings in four months. Service had writ The Trail of Ninety Eight and Rhymes of a Rolling Stone. Five books carry the tale: the story of Margot, the story of Hugh, the wheel, the vortex, and the man hunt.

A prologue opens in a shabby room. A boy sits in a corner, drawing, while his mother watches from her pillow. His father was an artist, she tells him, and died just before he was born. She came here hoping his people, so rich, so proud, would be glad to see the child. They cannot understand, she says. Home is Monaco, the great rock that rises from the sea.
69077-half-hours-on-the-quarter-deck-the:
Half Hours on the Quarter-Deck is a naval history for young readers in the Half Hour Library, running from the Spanish Armada to Sir Cloudesley Shovell. The series volumes, handsomely bound and fully illustrated, sold at two shillings and sixpence. Its companions include Half Hours in the Holy Land by Norman Macleod and Half Hours with a Naturalist by Wood. Half Hours Underground was by Charles Kingsley and others.

A notice preserved in the copy places this book in its line. It is the second of a series on a subject of the greatest interest to all young Englishmen: the naval history of England. To the sea, the writer says, England owes its greatness. The Anglo-Saxon race owes to it the possession of such large portions of the earth.
69303-michelangelo:
Edward C Strutt wrote this small life of Michelangelo for Bell's Miniature Series of Painters, printed by George Bell and Sons of London. First issued in January 1904, it was reprinted in 1908. The David at Florence stands as frontispiece. A list of books about the artist opens the volume, from Condivi's life to those of Symonds and Holroyd.

A chronology of the artist's life comes next, then the life itself, a study of his art, and notes on the plates. A list of his chief works in public galleries ends it. The life opens with a diary entry of his father, Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni, dated March 6, 1475, recording the birth of a son named Michelagnolo. The book packs a master's whole career into a pocket volume.
69716-life-and-labor-in-the-spirit-world:
Life and Labor in the Spirit World, published at Boston in 1885, describes the localities, employments, and conditions of the spheres beyond death. The accounts came through the medium Shelhamer, of the Banner of Light free circle, and are credited to her spirit band. Her guides told her the book would teach mortals what they could learn from no other source.

Shelhamer says the words themselves were chosen by the spirits, received in quiet seclusion. Chapters present spirit voices such as Violet and Echoes, meetings of missionary spirits, and spirits returning to comfort their mothers. The volume is a full specimen of American Spiritualist literature, when séances and spirit messages formed a popular religion of hope for the bereaved.
britannica-1911-abati-niccolo: Niccolo Abati, also written Dell' Abbato, is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry names a famed fresco painter of Modena, with dates 1512 to 1571. His best works stand at Modena and Bologna, it states. He went with Primaticcio to France and helped deck the palace at Fontainebleau across two decades. Skill in drawing, grace, and natural color mark his pictures, the entry holds. One oil at Dresden, the martyrdom of St Peter and St Paul, ranks among his finest easel pieces.
britannica-1911-accorso-accursius-marian:
Mariangelo Accorso (about 1490-1544) was an Italian critic born at Aquila in the kingdom of Naples. A great favourite of the emperor Charles V, he spent thirty-three years at that court and travelled on foreign missions. To perfect Greek and Latin he added several modern languages, and his travels gave him rare chances to discover and collate, or compare, ancient manuscripts.

Scholarship of that kind fills his record. His Diatribae on Ausonius, Solinus, and Ovid is called a monument of learning and critical skill. He first edited the Letters of Cassiodorus, and his edition of Ammianus Marcellinus added five books beyond any earlier one. Accused of plagiarism in his notes, he repudiated the charge with great energy.
britannica-1911-agostino-paolo:
Paolo Agostino (1593-1629) was an Italian musician. He was born at Valerano. Giovanni Battista Nanini was his teacher in music. Dedications in his mass books record that debt. He later became his master's son-in-law. Agostino succeeded Ugolini as conductor of the pope's orchestra. That orchestra served in St Peter's at Rome. The post was among Italy's most prestigious musical offices.

Compositions are his claim on memory. His works are numerous, the entry says. Great merit is claimed for them collectively. One piece receives special admiration by name. It is an Agnus Dei written for eight voices. Eight-part writing showed a master's command of counterpoint. Brief as the entry is, it fixes his posts. Rome's papal chapel defined his career wholly.
britannica-1911-almelo:
Almelo is a town in the province of Overysel, Holland. It lies north-west of Hengelo at the junction of two canals. The Overysel and Almelo canals meet there. Its population in 1900 was 9,957. The place is of considerable antiquity. It was the seat of an independent lordship before the fourteenth century. Real importance came only in the second half of the nineteenth century.

That rise came from Almelo's share in the industrial growth of the Twente district. The town possesses numerous cotton and damask factories. Public buildings include a town hall and a court house. There is also a corn exchange. Churches of various kinds and a synagogue stand there. The entry traces the lordship's owners as well. The lords of Heeckeren gained Rechteren by marriage in 1350. They gained a countship in 1711. Their line remains established at Almelo.
britannica-1911-armadillo:
Armadillo is an animal article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a group of small mail clad beasts of Central and South America. The name is Spanish. Their shell is a case of bone, part fixed plates and part loose bands that let the body bend.

The article describes how the beasts live. Horny scales lie over the bone plates of the shell. They eat roots, insects, worms, small reptiles, and dead flesh. Most kinds come out at night, though not all. They offer no fight when caught, the text says. Their defence is speed in digging and a hard grip in their holes. Kinds range from a giant beast near a yard long to very small ones. One group can roll itself into a tight ball.
britannica-1911-baccio-d-agnolo:
Baccio d'Agnolo (c. 1460-1543) was a Florentine wood-carver, sculptor, and architect, born Bartolommeo Baglioni and known by his shortened name, son of Angelo. He began in wood, carving much decoration for Santa Maria Novella and the Palazzo Vecchio between 1491 and 1502.

With his name made as a sculptor, Baccio turned to architecture. He helped restore the Palazzo Vecchio. In 1506 he was set to finish the drum of Florence cathedral's dome. Michelangelo's criticism stopped that work. He planned the Villa Borghese and the Bartolini palace, first house given columned fronts to doors and windows, a church-like novelty Florentines mocked. His studio drew Michelangelo, Sansovino, the Sangallo brothers, and the young Raphael.
britannica-1911-bartoli-daniello:
Daniello Bartoli (1608–1685), an Italian Jesuit priest born at Ferrara, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1623. Barred from the foreign mission field he had wanted, he won high standing instead as a preacher. He also taught rhetoric, the art of public speaking and writing, in Genoa, Florence, and Rome. Those cities, rather than distant missions, became the scene of his life's work.

Books carry Bartoli's reputation in the entry. Writing in Italian, he produced The Learned Man as an answer to the wide reading of romances. His larger work was a history of his order in six volumes, published at Rome from 1650 to 1673. The entry calls it especially informative about the early work of the Jesuits in Asia. Bartoli died at Rome, and collected editions of his works later ran to twelve volumes at Turin and fifty at Florence.
britannica-1911-baylo:
Baylo was the title of the Venetian representative at Constantinople, the Ottoman capital. The word comes from Latin forms linked to bailiff, and in Italian it appears as balio. At first the baylo acted much like a consul-general for Venice there.

From the 1600s on, the post also carried the rank and duties of a top-class diplomatic agent. A quoted account by A. de Wicquefort says the baylo served as consul and judge too. He settled cases among his own people and among all merchants who traded in the Levant under the flag of St Mark.
britannica-1911-carballo:
Carballo is a town of north-western Spain. It stands in the province of Corunna, in Galicia. It lies on the right bank of the river Allones. The city of Corunna is 20 miles north-east of it. Its population in 1900 was 13,032. This very short 1911 Britannica entry gives the town's plain facts. It adds its one line of local business.

Carballo is the central market of its district. That district is a thriving agricultural one, the entry says. Farmers bring their produce to the town to trade. Across the river stands San Juan de Carballo. Hot sulphurous springs rise at that village. The springs are the entry's one further point of interest. The whole notice runs to three short sentences. It gives the market role and the springs, and nothing more.
britannica-1911-cattaneo-carlo:
Carlo Cattaneo lived from 1801 to 1869 and was an Italian thinker and patriot. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry traces his life from youth to old age. As a young man he joined the Carbonari in Lombardy. He then turned to study and sought to draw Italians toward science and clear fact.

Much of the entry covers the revolt of 1848 in Milan. Cattaneo helped lead the Five Days rising against Austria. He sat on the war council at Casa Taverna and urged a hard line. He refused terms that would let the foe stay in Lombardy. Readers get a close look at a firm republican mind at work.
britannica-1911-cignani-carlo:
Cignani, Carlo (1628–1719) was an Italian painter, born of a noble family at Bologna, where he studied under Battista Cairo and then under Francesco Albani. Albani's most famous disciple, he was yet deeply shaped by Correggio as well. His greatest work, the Assumption of the Virgin round a cupola at Forlì, took some twenty years. That fresco plainly follows Correggio's more renowned cupola at Parma, the entry says.

Elaborate finish and bold artifice in colour mark the disciple of Albani, but Cignani gave his work a more thoughtful character than either model. Amiable, modest and generous as a man, he refused honours from princes and lived and died an artist. Envy led some enemies to deface certain works of his. His school at Bologna followed him when he removed to Forlì, and his son and nephew also painted.
britannica-1911-citta-di-castello:
Città di Castello is a town and episcopal see of Umbria, Italy, in the province of Perugia, on the left bank of the Tiber at 945 feet. It lies 38 miles east of Arezzo by rail, and its town people numbered 6,096 in 1901, with 26,885 in the commune. Inscriptions show it occupies the site of ancient Tifernum Tiberinum, near which Pliny had a villa. No remains of that town exist above ground today.

Totila devastated the town, yet it recovered and appears as Castrum Felicitatis late in the 8th century, with a bishopric from the 7th. Emperor and Church held it in turn until the Vitelli took it in 1468, after whose line died out it returned to the Church. Walls of 1518 ring its rectangle, and fine Renaissance palaces of the Vitelli stand inside. Some of Raphael's earliest works were painted for its churches, but none remains there.
britannica-1911-clavicembalo: Clavicembalo is the subject of a short 1911 Britannica entry on a keyboard instrument of old Europe. Its strings are plucked by small quills or bits of leather. The name joins the Latin word for a key with the word cymbal. Cymbal was the old term for the dulcimer in Europe. That is how it came to sit in the long name. Forms of the name in English, Flemish, and Spanish are given. The entry points readers to the pianoforte, spinet, and virginal.
britannica-1911-colonna-giovanni-paolo:
Giovanni Paolo Colonna (about 1637–1695) was an Italian musician born and raised in Bologna. He learned from Filippuzzi at home, then from Abbatini and Benevoli in Rome. In Rome he served for a time as organist at Saint Apollinare. A dated poem of praise shows that he made his mark as a composer by 1659.

That same year he became organist at Saint Petronio in Bologna. On 1 November 1674 he rose to chapel-master there. He also led the Philharmonic Academy of Bologna as president. Most of his work serves the church. Psalm settings for three to eight voices stand beside masses and motets. He wrote one opera, Amilcare, and one oratorio. The emperor Leopold I kept a copy of each piece he wrote. Vienna thus holds more than 83 of his church works. His style is called dignified in the main.
britannica-1911-corelli-arcangelo:
Arcangelo Corelli (1653-1713), an Italian violin player and composer, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Fusignano near Imola in February 1653. Of his life little is known, the entry says. His master on the violin was Bassani, and a famed singer of the pope's chapel taught him composition.

His first clear success came in Paris at the age of nineteen, and it made his name across Europe. From Paris he went to Germany and spent time in the service of the prince of Bavaria. By 1685 he was in Rome, leading the festival music for Queen Christine of Sweden and standing high with a great cardinal. He later lived in that cardinal's palace. The style of playing he set was kept alive by his pupils, among them Geminiani and Locatelli.
britannica-1911-crivelli-carlo:
Carlo Crivelli was a Venetian painter born in the earlier part of the 1400s. The only firm dates are 1468 and 1493, the earliest and latest years signed on his pictures. Though born in Venice, he worked chiefly in the March of Ancona, in and near Ascoli. He is said to have studied under Jacobello del Fiore. From 1490 he added the word Miles to his signature, having been knighted by Ferdinand II of Naples.

Crivelli painted in tempera only and shows best in subject pictures of moderate size. He liked landscape backgrounds and set fruits and flowers, above all the peach, as hanging garlands in his scenes. The entry calls his style hard in form and stern in feature, yet warm and distinct in colour. His Annunciation and Beato Ferretti hang in the National Gallery in London. Other named works sit at Berlin, in the Vatican, and in the Brera at Milan.
britannica-1911-dandolo:
Dandolo is the name of one of the great patrician families of Venice, first recorded among the electors of the first doge in 697. The family gave Venice four doges. The first and most famous was Enrico Dandolo, elected on 1 January 1193. Over seventy and of very weak sight, he still proved an energetic and able ruler. His first care was to restore Venetian power over the Dalmatians, though Zara held out against him.

In 1201 crusaders asked Venice for ships to carry 4,500 horse and 29,000 foot to Palestine, at 85,000 marks with half of all conquests. The crusaders could not pay, and Dandolo proposed that they first help him take Zara, with payment put off. The fleet of three hundred sail left on 8 October 1202 with the old doge in command.
britannica-1911-ermelo:
Ermelo is a district and a town of the Transvaal, and the entry treats both in a short notice. The district lies in the south-east of the province and is crossed by the Drakensberg. In it are Lake Chrissie, the only true lake in the country, and the sources of four rivers. The Vaal, Olifants, Komati, and Usuto all rise within 30 miles of one another there.

The region stands at a general height of about 5500 feet. It is fine farming and grazing country, and it also holds valuable minerals, including coal and gold. Ermelo town had 1451 people in 1904. It stands by rail 175 miles south-east of Johannesburg and 74 miles south-south-west of Machadodorp, on the Pretoria to Delagoa Bay line. A government experimental farm is kept at the town. That farm has some 1000 acres of plantations, the entry adds, closing a compact sketch of a high farming district.
britannica-1911-fabbroni-angelo:
Angelo Fabbroni, an Italian biographer who lived from 1732 to 1803, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Marradi in Tuscany and studied at Faenza. He then entered the Roman college set up for young Tuscans. After his studies he stayed in Rome, where the Jansenist scholar Bottari won him a canonry.

Fabbroni was chosen to preach in the pontifical chapel before Benedict the Fourteenth, and made so good an impression that the pope settled an annuity on him. That income freed him to give his whole time to study. He was close to Leopold, grand duke of Tuscany, though the Jesuits disliked his Jansenist views. In 1771 he began a literary journal, which he kept up until 1796. In Paris he met Condorcet, Diderot, and Rousseau. His chief work is a set of lives of notable Italians in twenty volumes.
britannica-1911-fallopius-gabriello:
Gabriello Fallopius, an Italian anatomist who lived from 1523 to 1562, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Modena about the year 1523. There he became a canon of the cathedral in his youth. He studied medicine at the university of Ferrara.

After a tour of Europe, Fallopius taught anatomy at Ferrara. He moved on to Pisa, and from there to Padua by a duke's call. At Padua he held the chairs of anatomy and surgery and of botany together. He also superintended the new botanical garden of that city. He died at Padua in October 1562, still in his thirties. Only one treatise of his appeared in his lifetime. Those Anatomical Observations were printed at Venice in 1561. His collected genuine works followed at Venice in 1584, long after his death.
britannica-1911-farini-luigi-carlo:
Luigi Carlo Farini (1812–1866), Italian statesman and historian, was born at Russi near Ravenna on 22 October 1812. A brilliant Bologna course broke off for the revolution of 1831. He then practised medicine at Russi and Ravenna and built a reputation. In 1843 his politics drew police suspicion, and he was expelled from the papal states. He lived in Florence and Paris, travelling as physician to Prince Jerome Bonaparte.

When Pius IX opened with liberal leanings, Farini returned as secretary-general to the interior minister in March 1848. He resigned on 29 April when the pope refused war on Austria. After the republic and the pope's return he withdrew to Turin. There he backed the House of Savoy in Cavour's press. His chief work, Lo Stato Romano dal 1815 al 1850, filled four volumes in 1850. He served as minister of public instruction in 1851–1852.
britannica-1911-fea-carlo:
Carlo Fea (1753-1836), Italian archaeologist, was born at Pigna in Piedmont on 2 February 1753 and studied law in Rome, taking his doctorate at the university of La Sapienza. Archaeology gradually took over his attention, and in 1798 he took orders to gain better chances for research. Driven to Florence for political reasons, he returned in 1799 and was jailed by the Neapolitans then holding Rome as a Jacobin.

Freed soon after, Fea became Commissario delle Antichita and librarian to Prince Chigi. He revised an Italian translation of Winckelmann's History of Art with notes, and annotated works by Bianconi. His own writings include a miscellany of philology and antiquities, a defence of the Pantheon's link to Agrippa, fragments of consular lists, inscriptions of public monuments, and a description of Rome. He died at Rome on 18 March 1836, having spent his later career among the city's antiquities.
britannica-1911-federici-camillo:
Camillo Federici (1749-1802), Italian dramatist and actor, was born at Garessio in Piedmont on 9 April 1749. His real name was Giovanni Battista Viassolo; Federici came from the title of an early piece, Camillo e Federico, and passed to his children. Educated at Turin, he loved literature and the theatre from youth. Praise for his first attempts fixed his career, and he worked with several companies as both writer and actor.

Federici married happily in 1777, left the stage, and settled at Padua to write. His many comedies spread his fame across Italy and for a time eclipsed his predecessors. Most are melodramatic, and he leaned on the moral tone found in Schiller, Iffland and Kotzebue. A merchant friend, Francis Barisan, kept him writing for a private theatre. Illness struck in 1791 and again as he prepared a collected edition. He died at Padua on 23 December 1802.
britannica-1911-filangieri-carlo:
Carlo Filangieri, prince of Satriano, a Neapolitan soldier and statesman who lived from 1784 to 1867, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Gaetano Filangieri, a famed thinker and jurist. At fifteen Carlo chose a soldier's life and won a place at the Military Academy in Paris. Napoleon, then first consul, received him in person.

In 1803 he got a commission in a foot regiment and fought in the campaign of 1805. He served at Ulm and Austerlitz, where he was wounded more than once and promoted. He came back to Naples in 1806 to fight the Bourbons and Austrians, and later served in Spain. Under Murat he rose to general and fought in Calabria and at Messina. He was badly wounded at the Panaro in 1815, in Murat's last campaign against Austria.
britannica-1911-folengo-teofilo:
Teofilo Folengo (1491-1544), known as Merlino Coccajo, was one of the chief Italian macaronic poets, mixing Latin with vernacular words for comic effect. He was born of noble parentage at Cipada near Mantua on 8 November 1491. From infancy he showed a lively mind and a rare cleverness at making verses. At sixteen he entered the monastery of Monte Casino near Brescia. Eighteen months later he became a professed Benedictine, and for a few years his monk's life ran regularly enough.

About 1516 Folengo left the cloister for the company of a well-born young woman, Girolama Dieda. They wandered the country for years, often in great poverty, living on his talent for verse. His first publication was the Macaronicon of Merlino Coccajo, the work that made his name. The entry follows his Latin verse and his macaronic poems, part mock-heroic and part satire.
britannica-1911-forner-juan-bautista-pab:
Juan Bautista Pablo Forner, a Spanish satirist and scholar who lived from 1756 to 1799, is covered in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Merida on February 23, 1756. He studied at Salamanca and was called to the bar at Madrid in 1783.

Forner then fought a long string of print wars with other writers. He used many false names, and his attacks were so harsh that he was banned from such work. He was moved to a legal post at Seville, then made crown prosecutor at Madrid in 1796. The piece praises his defense of Spain and its writing, printed in 1787, as learned and strong.
britannica-1911-fresnillo:
Fresnillo is a town of the state of Zacatecas, Mexico, 37 miles north-west of the city of Zacatecas on a branch of the Santiago river. It held 6309 people in 1900 and stands about 7700 feet above the sea on a fertile plain between the Santa Cruz and Zacatecas ranges. The climate is temperate, and the farms around raise Indian corn and wheat.

The town's chief distinction is its school of mines, founded in 1853. Large amalgam works there treat silver ores from the mines of the neighbouring Proaño hill. Those mines were found in 1569 and for a time ranked among the richest in Mexico, but output fell sharply after the best deposits were reached in 1833. A station on the Mexican Central railway serves the town.
britannica-1911-giacometti-paolo:
Italian playwright Paolo Giacometti, born at Novi Ligure in eighteen sixteen, is given a brief life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was trained in law at Genoa. At age twenty he had some luck with a play called Rosilda. After that he gave his life to the stage.

Hard times led him to write for touring groups that moved from town to town. He wrote a great deal, and top actors made many plays a hit. Works named as among his best span from eighteen fifty to eighteen eighty. They include La Donna, Giuditta, Sofocle, and La Morte civile. A set of his works came out at Milan in eight books.
britannica-1911-godollo:
Godollo is a market town of Hungary, in the county of Pest-Pilis-Solt-Kiskun, 23 miles north-east of Budapest by rail. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 5,875 people in 1900. It is the summer residence of the Hungarian royal family.

The royal castle was built in the second half of the 18th century by Prince Anton Grassalkovich. Castle and beautiful domain were presented by the Hungarian nation to King Francis Joseph I after the coronation of 1867. Stags and wild boars fill the park in great number. The entry calls the town a favourite summer resort for the people of Budapest. Nearby stands Maria-Besnyo, a famous place of pilgrimage with a fine Franciscan monastery holding the Grassalkovich family tombs.
britannica-1911-goldoni-carlo:
Carlo Goldoni was an Italian writer of plays held as the true founder of new gay plays in Italy, who lived from seventeen seven to seventeen ninety-three. He was born at Venice. His first toys were puppets that he made dance. His first books were plays, and at age eight he tried to sketch a play of his own.

His father set him to learn the heal art and law in turn, but stage love won each time. He ran off with a troupe of players as a youth. A sharp verse that stung great homes drove him from one town. His first grave plays met with mixed luck.
britannica-1911-hunyadi-laszlo:
Laszlo Hunyadi, who lived from 1433 to 1457, was a Hungarian lord and soldier. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells his brief and violent story. He was the eldest son of Janos Hunyadi, the famed war leader. As a boy he rode on campaign with his father.

After his father died in 1456, foes charged Laszlo with state debts. He cleared himself at a diet and kept command of Belgrade. A rival lord tried to kill him there and was cut down instead. The young king swore to shield the whole family. Weeks later the king had him seized at Buda on a plot charge. With no fair trial held, he was beheaded in March 1457.
britannica-1911-juarez-benito-pablo:
Benito Pablo Juárez (1806–1872), president of Mexico, was born near Ixtlan in the state of Oajaca on the 21st of March 1806, of full Indian blood. Left poor by his father's death, he gained schooling through a kind friar and then studied law. He began to practise in 1834 and rose fast as a voice for liberal views.

He governed Oajaca from 1847 to 1852, and was banished by Santa Anna in 1853. Back in 1855, he became minister of justice, then chief justice. When Comonfort was replaced in 1858, Juárez claimed the presidency by right of his office, and by 1861 had won it and been elected by congress. His halt on debt payments brought foreign troops to Mexico. France stayed, made war, and set Maximilian on a throne. Juárez held out in the north until Maximilian was taken and shot in 1867.
britannica-1911-la-tour-d-auvergne-theop:
Théophile Malo La Tour d'Auvergne (1743–1800), French soldier, was born at Carhaix in Brittany on the 23rd of December 1743, the son of an advocate named Corret. Set on a military career, he got himself enlisted in the Maison du Roi on a certificate of nobility signed by his friends. In 1771 he took the surname La Tour d'Auvergne, as a descendant of an illegitimate half-brother of Turenne.

Years of routine service were broken by volunteering with the Franco-Spanish expedition to Minorca in 1781, after which he refused promotion into the Spanish army rather than change allegiance. Made captain in 1784 and given the cross of St Louis in 1791, he opposed his brother officers' wish to emigrate rather than swear to the constitution. In 1792 he published a work on the Bretons. He won notice for courage in the Alps and harder fighting in the Pyrenees, yet declined promotion to colonel.
britannica-1911-mantegazza-paolo:
Paolo Mantegazza, an Italian physiologist and anthropologist who lived from 1831 to 1910, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Monza in October 1831. He studied at Pisa and Milan. He took his medical degree at Pavia in 1854.

After travel in Europe, India, and America, he practised as a doctor in Argentina and Paraguay. Back in Italy in 1858, he became a surgeon at Milan Hospital. He also held a chair in general pathology at Pavia. In 1870 he was named professor of anthropology at Florence. There he founded the first museum of anthropology and ethnology in Italy. He later founded the Italian Anthropological Society. He also sat in parliament as deputy for Monza for a decade. The life joins field travel, medicine, and the new science of man.
britannica-1911-masaniello:
Masaniello, a short form of Tommaso Aniello, was a fisherman of Amalfi who lived from 1622 to 1647. His revolt is told in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Bad rule and hard taxes had bred unrest through the two Sicilies. A revolt broke at Palermo in May 1647, and Naples rose next.

The spark in Naples was a new tax on fruit, the food of the poor. The rise began on the seventh of July with a clash at the city gates between fruit sellers and customs men. The crowd burnt the customs house and forced its way into the palace of the viceroy. Masaniello took command of the crowd. Dressed as a fisherman, he held court from a wood stage by his house and sought to curb its rage. The mob chose him captain-general of the city.
britannica-1911-matteucci-carlo:
Carlo Matteucci is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an Italian physicist. He lived from 1811 to 1868. He was born at Forli on the twentieth of June 1811. He attended the Ecole Polytechnique at Paris in his youth. He became professor of physics at Bologna in 1832. He then held chairs at Ravenna and at Pisa. From 1847 he took an active part in politics.

In 1860 he was chosen an Italian senator. At the same time he became inspector general of telegraph lines. Two years later he was minister of education of Italy. He died near Leghorn in June of 1868. He was the author of four scientific treatises in all. His lectures on physics fill two volumes from Pisa. Another work treats the physical chemistry of living bodies. A manual of electric telegraphy is also listed. His numerous papers appeared in a French journal of physics.
britannica-1911-michelangelo:
Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564) was the most famous of the great Florentine artists of the Renaissance, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his family. He was the son of Ludovico Buonarroti, a poor gentleman of Florence. His mother was Francesca dei Neri. The Buonarroti Simoni were an old Florentine stock of the Guelf faction.

In the days of his fame, a link was claimed with the counts of Canossa. Both sides admitted that link at the time. The entry states flatly that it has no basis in fact. Ludovico could barely live on the income of his estate. He boasted that he had never stooped to trade or craft work to add to it. The favour of the Medici gained him short posts in minor offices of state.
britannica-1911-milo:
Milo of Crotona, a Greek strong man of the sixth century before the common count, is covered in a short entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was crowned six times at the Olympic games for wrestling. He won six more crowns at the Pythian games. His feats of strength were famed through the known world.

One famed feat was to carry an ox on his back through the race ground at Olympia. In his home city he was held in honor. He led the army that beat the folk of Sybaris in five eleven. The tale of his death points a moral. He tried to tear a tree that wood men had split with a wedge. The wedge fell out and the tree shut on his hand. Wolves then ate him where he stood trapped. His name grew to a byword for strength.
britannica-1911-passaglia-carlo:
Carlo Passaglia lived from 1812 to 1887 and was an Italian divine of Rome. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Lucca, where he was born in May 1812. Set for the priesthood from youth, he trained with the Jesuits at fifteen. He took degrees in math, in thought, and in the study of God. All three came from the university of Rome in his student years.

In 1844 he was made a teacher at the Collegio Romano in Rome. The next year he took his vows as a Jesuit in the order. Driven from Rome in 1848, he paid a short visit to England. Back in Italy he helped found the Jesuit journal Civilta Cattolica. That journal grew famed as the voice of the order in print.
britannica-1911-pergolesi-michael-angelo:
Michael Angelo Pergolesi was an Italian decorative artist of the 1700s. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that facts on his life are near wholly lacking. Like Cipriani, he was drawn to England by Robert Adam. He worked so much for the Adam brothers that their style bears his stamp. His range matched theirs: furniture, fireplaces, ceilings, lights, doors, and wall work.

In low relief plaster work he had no peer of his day. He loved urns, sphinxes, and twined gryphons in his designs. Cupids with bows and torches recur, with trophies of arms and music. Flowering scroll work frames the whole, graceful if at times thin. Wall and ceiling centres often held painted scenes by Cipriani or Kauffmann. Those figures were copied onto satinwood furniture of the age. His table tops and cabinets set the mark for dainty taste.
britannica-1911-piccolo:
Piccolo is a small flute pitched one octave higher than the concert flute. Its music entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is less than half the size of the large flute in build. Its build and sound rules match those of the flute in most ways.

The piccolo lacks the tail piece that gives the flute its low notes. It is the highest voice in the orchestra, save for rare violin tones. Music for it is written one octave low to dodge ledger lines. Composers use its shrill tone for storm winds in Beethoven and Wagner works. Verdi used it for comic effect in Falstaff, his late opera work.
britannica-1911-pollaiuolo:
Pollaiuolo is the nickname of two brothers of Florence who shaped Italian art. The 1911 Britannica entry names them Antonio and Piero Benci. Their father was a poulterer, which gave the pair their famed name. The nephew Simone bore that same nickname in his own day. Their work falls in the great bloom of art in the 1400s.

Antonio, born in 1429, excelled as sculptor, jeweller, painter, and engraver. He did much to perfect the art of enamelling in metal. His Saint Sebastian of 1475 hangs now in London's National Gallery. As a worker in bronze and metal he won his top fame. Which works are his and which are Piero's stays in doubt.
britannica-1911-sangallo:
Sangallo, the family name of a Florentine line famed in the fine arts, is covered in a 1911 Britannica article. The first man treated is Giuliano di Sangallo, who lived from 1445 to 1516. He was a builder, sculptor, and army engineer. His father also built for Cosimo de' Medici.

Giuliano worked chiefly for Lorenzo the Magnificent in his early years. He built a fine palace at Poggio a Cajano, begun in 1485. He also made the walls of Florence and other towns stronger. His name came from a friary he built by the San Gallo gate. Later he built a dome at Loreto and worked in Rome for two popes.
britannica-1911-sordello:
Sordello was a troubadour of the thirteenth century, born at Mantua in Italy. Dante praised him in one work and made him a mark of love of country in the Purgatorio. Robert Browning also made him the hero of a well known poem. The article warns that the real man fits these grand views poorly. Still, he was the most famed of the Italian troubadours of his day.

The facts of his life are rough ones. About 1220 he shows up in a tavern brawl at Florence. In 1226, at the court of Verona, he ran off with his master's wife at her brother's urging. The scandal drove him to flee to Provence in 1229. He later served Charles of Anjou and was held prisoner at Naples in 1266.
britannica-1911-spagna-lo:
Lo Spagna (died about 1529) is the name given to the Italian painter Giovanni di Pietro. The name comes from his Spanish birth. He was one of the chief followers of Perugino. The famed Sposalizio, the marriage of Joseph and Mary, in the Caen museum was once given to Perugino. It is now credited to Lo Spagna. Nothing at all is known of his early life.

Critics note a lack of a strong stamp of his own in his style. It reads like a weaker copy of the early Raphael and of Pinturicchio. Among his panel works are a Nativity in the Vatican and an Adoration of the Magi at Berlin. In 1510 he painted much wall work at Todi, and more near Trevi in 1512. His chief wall works were at Assisi and Spoleto. Spoleto gave him the freedom of the city in 1516 in thanks.
britannica-1911-torcello:
Torcello is a place article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an island in the lagoons of Venice, in Italy. It lies some six miles north-west of Venice, in the commune of Burano. In the early middle ages it was a thriving city. Now it has only a few houses and two churches of note.

The old cathedral of Saint Mary was founded in the seventh century. The present basilica dates from 864, and its nave was restored in 1008. Inside are large mosaics of the twelfth century, strongly Byzantine in style. Those on the west wall show the Resurrection and the Last Judgment. The priests' seats rise in steps round the apse, with the bishop's throne at the centre. Close by stands Saint Fosca, a twelfth-century church planned for a dome that was never built.
britannica-1911-water-polo:
Water polo is a game that has done much to advance swimming with the public. It has also improved the stamina of swimmers who play it, the entry says. The game is played in a bath or in open water by two teams. Each team holds seven players a side in the water at once. The field of play is set between set limits of length and width.

The ball must be round, fully blown up, and waterproof in its making. No strapped seams may show outside, and no grease may be placed on it. The goals are ten feet wide, with a cross bar at a set height. A match lasts fourteen minutes, played as seven minutes each way. Officials are a referee, a time keeper, and two goal scorers. A goal counts when the whole ball passes between the posts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adrian-of-cas:
Adrian of Castello, also called de Corneto from his Tuscan birthplace, was an Italian prelate famed as statesman and learning's reviver, born about 1460, who died about 1521. Innocent VIII sent him as nuncio to Scotland in 1488, but recalled him on news of James III's death. Adrian had reached England and won Henry VII's favour, becoming his agent at Rome.

He went back to England as Peter's-pence collector in 1489, gained a St. Paul's prebend and a London rectory, and served in the papal treasury and as Henry's ambassador. Alexander VI made him cardinal in 1503, and he became Bishop of Hereford in 1502 and of Bath and Wells in 1504, though he never occupied the latter. Implicated in 1517 in a plot to poison Leo X, he confessed, was forgiven, fled to Venice, and was degraded from the cardinalate in 1518.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Oslo occupied part of the site of Christiania, founded in 1624. After Hamar was formed in 1152, Oslo was limited to Christiania, Smaalenene, Jarlsberg and Laurvik, and Akershus in Norway, with Goteborg and Bohus in Sweden. Rudolf, a court bishop brought by Saint Olave from Rouen, worked at Sarpsborg from 1015 to 1030, but Asgaut, from 1047 to 1072, is usually counted the first Bishop of Oslo.

Nicholas Arnesson, bishop from 1190 to 1225, played a great though unhappy part in Norwegian politics. Haakon, from 1248 to 1265, gave generously to his chapter before moving to Trondhjem. Solomon, from 1322 to 1352, was the only Norwegian bishop to survive the Black Death in 1349, and in 1350 he consecrated bishops for Bergen and Skalholt in Iceland. In 1352 Pope Clement VI made Gyrd Aslesson exchange sees with Sigfrid of Stavanger. Eystein, from 1385 to 1407, helped negotiate the union of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under Queen Margaret in 1397.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-and-p:
Antonio and Piero Benci Pollajuolo, Florentine brothers born in 1432 and 1443, took their name from their father's poultry trade. Antonio trained under Uccello and worked as painter, sculptor, and goldsmith, while Piero learned in his brother's studio. From 1465 they worked together, and both died at Rome and share one tomb in Saint Peter in Chains.

Antonio's own paintings include David and three labours of Hercules, small panels now at Berlin and the Uffizi. As a sculptor he cast the bronze tomb of Sixtus the Fourth in Saint Peter's, its portrait head crowned with the tiara. Piero painted altarpieces of his own, and the entry presents two brothers who joined craft, muscle, and devotion in Renaissance Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolome-est:
Bartolomé Esteban Murillo was a Spanish painter born at Seville in 1617, who died there in 1682. Esteban was his family name; Murillo, his mother's, he took by Andalusian custom. Orphaned at ten, he was raised by his barber uncle and studied under Juan del Castillo, a mediocre painter but good teacher. To live, he painted cheap sargas on rough canvas, sold at country fairs and shipped to America.

In Madrid, Velasquez, a fellow Sevillian, opened the royal galleries to him, where he studied Titian, Veronese, Tintoretto, and Rubens for three years. He returned to Seville in 1644 and left it only once more, for Cadiz in 1681, to paint a Capuchin altar he never finished. A fall from scaffolding or a serious illness ended that work, by differing accounts. His Immaculate Conceptions remain his most famed devotional works, genuinely religious in feeling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedetto-mar:
Benedetto Marcello, a Venetian composer and public servant, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Venice in 1696 and dead at Brescia in 1739, he mixed politics with art throughout his life. He served as provveditore, a Venetian overseer, at Pola, then as camerlengo, a finance officer, at Brescia, where failing health ended his service.

Music, though, is his lasting claim. Manuscripts of his musical theory and his operas survive in Venice, Dresden, and Brussels. His best work, by the entry's judgment, is his paraphrase of the Psalms, a setting of the biblical songs in verse. The piece sketches a nobleman who governed by day and composed at length.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benvenuto-tis:
Benvenuto Tisio, called Garofalo after his birthplace, was a painter of the Ferrara school, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Born in 1481, he died at Ferrara in 1559. With Mazzolino and Dosso Dossi he forms the modest trio of sixteenth-century Ferrarese painting, heir to an earlier school famed for the Schifanoja Palace frescoes.

Early promise showed in hunting and procession scenes painted with a romantic eye, learned under Panetti and Costa and coloured by Venetian lessons at Cremona. Three years in Rome then bent him toward Raphael and Michelangelo, a spell the entry judges costly to his own voice. His later work never quite regained its first freshness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernal-diaz-d:
