Bernal Díaz del Castillo, a Spanish chronicler of the conquest of Mexico, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Medina del Campo about 1498, he died after 1568. A common soldier of poor parents, he sailed to America in 1514, reached Yucatán in 1517, and marched into Mexico with Cortés.

He claims a part in 119 battles and was present at the fall of Mexico City, a claim the entry treats as a soldier's honest record. His True History, written late in life, answers more polished accounts with an eyewitness voice. The piece presents the conquest as one foot soldier saw and remembered it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-agostino-n:
Blessed Agostino Novello, born Matteo di Termini in Sicily during the early thirteenth century, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His village belonged to Palermo's archdiocese, so he is sometimes called Panormitano. His noble Catalan family schooled him carefully in the sciences of his day.

On entering religion he took the name Agostino, with Novello added for his learning and virtue. He served as a high official of the Augustinian order, then retired to a hermitage at San Leonardo, where miracles were reported at his tomb. The entry presents a scholar turned hermit, honoured by two cities claiming him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-buffalo:
Buffalo, a diocese set up on 23 April 1847, covers eight New York counties across 6,357 square miles, nearly a third of the state. Cut from the great New York diocese with its see on Lake Erie, it lost its eastern counties to Rochester in 1868 and four more after Bishop Ryan's death in 1896. Before white settlers came, Senecas and Cayugas of the Iroquois League held the region.

Seneca raids carried Huron Christian captives from Canada into a village called Saint Michael's, visited by Jesuits in 1656. Fremin built a chapel there in the fall of 1668 and said the first Mass on 3 November 1668. Pierron followed at Gannagaro, or Saint James, in 1671, while Carheil raised Saint Joseph's chapel among the Cayugas in November 1668. Other chapels, like the Immaculate Conception at Totiakton near Lima, served four or five flourishing Jesuit missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capaccio-and-:
Capaccio and Vallo form a suffragan diocese of Salerno in southern Italy, with the bishop residing at Vallo. Capaccio stands near the ruins of ancient Paestum. It is thought to have been built after Saracens destroyed Paestum in 915, when the see moved there. Its first known bishop was Arnolfo, present at the Lateran council of 1179.

Later bishops named in the entry include the zealous monk Pietro Matta de Haro, Tommaso Caraffa, and Giovanni della Pace, along with the learned Cardinal Francesco Maria Brancacci. Lelio Morello moved the bishop's residence to Dania under Sixtus V. The diocese counted 122,400 people with 102 parishes, 282 churches and chapels, and hundreds of priests, plus three religious houses for men.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cignani-famil:
An entry on the Cignani, three Bolognese painters of one family, headed by Carlo, born in 1628. A count of noble birth, Carlo studied under Albani, felt the Carracci strongly, and followed Correggio. His first major work decorated Cardinal Farnese's great salon at Bologna, and his plague scenes in San Michele in Bosco, each upheld by two angels of remarkable beauty, show Correggio's manner. A palace interior for the Duke of Parma won him knighthood.

Carlo's masterpiece, the Assumption of the Virgin, fills the cupola of Forlì cathedral, painted from 1681 to 1706. After it he held high town office and presided over Bologna's academy under Clement the Eleventh. His colour is suave, his drawing largely accurate, and his facility extraordinary, though grandeur outruns execution. He died at Forlì in 1719. His son Felice, born 1660, painted for pleasure from a large fortune, and his nephew Paolo, born 1709, left only three known paintings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-citta-di-cast:
Citta di Castello, in the province of Perugia in Umbria, stands on an Apennine slope near the Tiber, on the site of ancient Tifernum. Pliny built a splendid villa there. In 550 Fantalogus, acting for Totila, the Ostrogothic king, took and destroyed the city, later rebuilt around a castle, giving it its name. By Pepin's donation in 752 it came under the Holy See.

Later centuries saw Guelph and Ghibelline rule, a rising against the States of the Church in 1375, and capture by Braccio da Montone in 1420 under Martin the Fifth. Nicolo Vitelli ruled as tyrant until Sixtus the Fourth's siege in 1474 forced his surrender. The city also claims martyrs under Diocletian, its first-known bishop Ennodius in 465, and Pope Celestine the Second, born there. Its cathedral keeps a twelfth-century silver altar-front and a fifteenth-century crosier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-in-tr:
The Council in Trullo, a Constantinople synod of 692 under Justinian II, met in the domed hall that gave it its name. Called Quinisext, or Fifth-Sixth, it supplied the disciplinary canons the Fifth and Sixth General Councils had omitted. All 215 bishops in attendance were Eastern, and they issued 102 canons, largely reaffirming earlier ones.

Western churches never recognised those canons, which renewed old decrees, condemned the heresy of Honorius, and pressed Constantinople's customs on the whole Church. Celibacy rules drew the sharpest line: clerics below bishop might remain married, and none might separate a priest from his wife. Eastern Orthodoxy still counts the council ecumenical.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-enrico-dandol:
Enrico Dandolo was Doge of Venice from 1192 to 1205, dying at a hundred years old. He came from an electoral family descended from the twelve tribunes who chose the first doge in 697. A kinsman was Patriarch of Grado for fifty years. A man of uncommon physical and mental strength, he took the cross at nearly a hundred and led the expedition against Constantinople. He was a fearless knight and a diplomat, predominant in the Fourth Crusade.

He first appears in the war with Emperor Manuel Comnenus in 1171, when plague-struck Venetians lay at Chios and Dandolo was sent to Constantinople for peace. Tradition says the emperor burned out his eyes, though later writers hold he was partly blinded. Elected doge on 1 June 1192, he settled quarrels with Verona. He warred on Zara and the Pisans. He made a treaty with Emperor Alexis III in 1198, before Venice fell out with Alexis in 1201.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ernest-hello:
Ernest Hello, a French philosopher and essayist, was born at Lorient in Brittany on 4 November 1828 and died at Kéroman, near Lorient, on 14 July 1885. Delicate health dogged him from infancy, and it hampered his work badly while giving his writings their melancholy tone.

At school in Rennes, and later at the College Louis-le-Grand in Paris, he stood first in his classes. He graduated at fifteen. His father's wishes sent him to law, and brilliant examinations won his admission. Yet he refused the profession, because his comrades had decided that a lawyer could not in conscience defend an unjust cause. Admiration for Gratry and Lacordaire drew him toward theology. Abbé Baudry, afterwards Bishop and then a professor at Saint-Sulpice, instructed him in it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-estevan-cabri:
Estevan Cabrillo was a Portuguese in Spain's naval service, born at an unknown date and place, dead on San Bernardo on 3 January 1543. In 1541 Pedro de Alvarado gathered twelve vessels at Navidad, on Western Mexico's coast, for an expedition to the Moluccas. Alvarado was soon killed assaulting the rock of Nochiztlan, defended by hostile Indians. The Viceroy Mendoza sent most of the squadron under Villalobos to the Moluccas, and two large vessels north under Cabrillo.

Cabrillo sailed from Navidad in 1542, coasting slowly upwards owing to contrary winds. In his voyage he discovered Santa Catalina, the Santa Barbara channel, Monterey, Cape Mendocino, and the Oregon coast to latitude 43 degrees. Scurvy broke out violently, so he could make only a short stay on Oregon and Northern California shores, and had to turn back. His treatment of the aborigines was particularly kind and generous.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faustino-arev:
Faustino Arevalo was a learned Spanish Jesuit who wrote hymns and studied the early Fathers. Born in 1747, he joined the Society in 1761 and was sent to Italy. Lorenzana, his patron, paid for his books and put him in charge of them. Arevalo later served the pope as hymn writer, theologian, and adviser in Rome.

His Hymnodia Hispanica of 1786 gave old Spanish hymns back their true metrical form. He also put out new texts of Prudentius, Dracontius, Juvencus, and Sedulius. Called back to Spain in 1815, he led the Castille province from 1820. Arevalo died at Madrid in 1824, famed for deep and scholarly learning and love of Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gasparo-molo:
Gasparo Molo, an Italian goldsmith and medalist of the seventeenth century, cut the dies of popes and princes. Born near Como or Lugano, he worked at Milan and Mantua, then at Florence from 1608 as master of the mint stamps. His medals for Cosimo II's marriage and accession in 1609 made his name, and he cut talers and merit medals for the grand duke.

About 1623 Molo moved to Rome as die-cutter at the papal mint, striking coins and medals under Urban VIII, Innocent X, and Alexander VII into 1664. A faithful portraitist and fine figure composer, he favored the stamped medal over the cast, and his stamped work ranks among the best of its age. His pupil Hamerani, founder of a long line of mint artists, carried his school forward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista Castello, called Il Bergamasco, was an Italian painter, sculptor, and architect born at Gandino in 1509, who died at Madrid in 1579. Left unprotected at Genoa as a young man, he won the protection of Tobia Pallavicino, who sent him to Rome to study the masters. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows him from Genoa palaces to the Spanish court.

Back in Genoa he decorated his protector's palace and painted the martyrdom of St. Sebastian. He worked with Luca Cambiaso in the Nunziata di Portoria. At Gorlago he painted scenes from the Iliad in the Lanzi Palace hall. Invited to Spain by Philip II in 1567, he adorned the Pardo with Ovidian subjects, worked at the Escorial, and died as architect of the royal palace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isleta-pueblo:
Two pueblos of the ancient Tigua people share the name Isleta, and this entry tells them apart. The older and chief town stands on the Rio Grande's west bank about twelve miles below Albuquerque, New Mexico. Its offshoot, Isleta del Sur, lies on the Texas side a few miles below El Paso. Spaniards named the first for its tongue of land jutting into the stream, while the native name Shiewhibak points to a knife used in a ceremonial foot race.

Coronado first entered Isleta in 1540, Espejo followed in 1582–83 seeking three murdered Franciscans, and before 1629 it housed the Franciscan mission of San Antonio. Later it sheltered refugees from outlying pueblos. The entry blends Spanish exploration, mission planting, and Tigua life into a short frontier history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jemez-pueblo:
Jemez Pueblo, an Indigenous town on the north bank of the Jemez River some twenty miles northwest of Bernalillo in New Mexico, shelters the last remnant of a people. They held some ten villages when Spaniards first met them in 1541. Neighbours named them Jemez; they call their town Walatoa, Bear Village.

Coronado entered their country in 1541, and Franciscans gathered them into two mission villages about 1618. After joining the great Pueblo rising of 1680, they were stormed by Vargas in 1694, fled to the Navajo after a 1696 revolt. They later returned to build their present pueblo. Smallpox in 1728 and 1780 cut them hard, leaving about five hundred souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-dicas:
Juan de Dicastillo was a Spanish Jesuit theologian born at Naples in 1584 to Spanish parents. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1600 and taught theology for twenty-five years at Toledo, Murcia, and Vienna. In moral questions he followed the probabilists, who held that a probable opinion may be safely followed.

His chief works treat justice and the cardinal virtues, the sacraments in general, oaths and church censures, and the Incarnation, all published at Antwerp between 1641 and 1662. Dicastillo died at Ingolstadt in 1653. The entry lists his books as the solid output of a long teaching career rather than a single famous work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ludovicus-a-s:
Ludovicus a S. Carolo, also known as Ludovicus Jacob, was a French Carmelite writer and librarian, born at Chalons in 1608 and dead at Paris in 1670. Son of Jean Jacob, he joined the Old Observance Carmelites in his home town and professed in 1626.

In Italy in 1639 he fell in love with inscriptions, lamenting their wholesale ruin in the catacombs, and finished Naude's Bibliotheca Pontificia at Rome. Back in France he served Cardinal de Retz and President Harlay as librarian, and became royal councillor and almoner. He also launched the first yearly lists of printed books, Paris lists for 1643 to 1645, a trade his successors still follow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luis-antonio-:
Luis Antonio Arguello was a governor of California, born at San Francisco in 1784 and dead there in 1830. His family ranked among the most influential in early California, and his father served as acting governor in 1814 and 1815, then governor of Lower California to 1822.

Luis succeeded his father as comandante in 1806, became captain in 1818, and governed from November 1822 to 1825. He was the only governor under the Mexican Empire and the first California native to hold the office. In 1821 he led the famed expedition to the Columbia, the widest Spanish exploration of the north country ever made from California, and left a name for honesty, ability, and kindness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marco-polo:
Marco Polo was a Venetian traveller, born in 1254 and dead there in 1324. His father Nicolo and uncle Matteo, sons of the patrician Andrea Polo, traded at Constantinople and Sudak in the Crimea. About 1255 they left Constantinople with jewels for Barka, Mongol Khan of Kipchak, who paid them well.

War with Hulagu of Persia stranded them, and they pushed east to Bokhara, staying three years. Envoys of Hulagu to the Great Khan carried them onward, and after three years' travel they reached Acre in 1269 with a Mongol baron. Marco soon won Kublai's affection, learning four Tatar tongues and scripts. Home again, the family looked and dressed like Tatars and had nearly lost their Venetian speech. Marco's Book, dictated to Rusticiano in French, tells the journeys, Kublai's realm, and the failed sea attack on Japan, surviving in eighty-five manuscripts with notable differences.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matteo-bandel:
Matteo Bandello was born at Castelnuovo di Scrivia in Piedmont in 1480 and died as Bishop of Agen, France, in 1565, though other sources give 1485 to 1561. He joined the Dominicans, but his life and writings show slight religious trace. He is best known by his Novelle, 214 tales in three volumes at Lyons in 1554, with a fourth in 1573.

These tales display real literary skill but do the churchman no credit, many being perverse accounts of horrors and wickedness. Many were translated into English by Painter and gave themes to Elizabethan dramatists. Most likely through that channel Shakespeare learned the Romeo and Juliet story. Byron later took up Bandello's Parisina tale. The best Novelle edition is Silvestri's Milan edition of 1813 to 1814 in nine volumes. Some tales appear in the Tesoro dei Novellieri Italiani of Paris, 1847, and some were translated by Roscoe in Italian Novelists of 1825.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mazzara-del-v:
Mazzara del Vallo, a diocese in the province of Trapani, Sicily, sits on the Mediterranean at the mouth of the Mazzara River. The town trades largely in lemons, boasts mineral springs nearby, and stands on the site of ancient Selinus's market port. A Megarian colony settled it in 630 B.C. Carthage took it in 409 B.C., and in 249 it was razed, its people deported to Lilybaeum.

A new town grew around the port, fell to the Saracens in 827, and became capital of one of their three Sicilian valli. Count Roger routed the Saracens there in 1075, and the see of Lilybaeum moved to Mazzara. Its bishops include Paschasinus, legate at Chalcedon, Stefano de Ferro, the first bishop in 1093, Cardinal Bessarion, and founders of cathedral, library, and seminary. The entry traces the see through conquest and rebuilding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-othlo:
Othlo, also spelled Otloh, was a Benedictine monk of Saint Emmeram's at Ratisbon, born in 1013 in the Diocese of Freising and dead in 1072. Schooled at Tegernsee and Hersfeld, Bishop Meginhard summoned him to Wuerzburg for his skill in writing. He entered the order in 1032, became dean in 1055, and took charge of the monastic school. To escape Bishop Otto's oppression he fled to Fulda in 1062, returning to Ratisbon in 1067.

Young Othlo loved the classics, above all Lucan, but later judged them unfit for religious minds and sought to replace pagan authors with his own edifying writings. Modest and pious, he opposed dialectics as bondage to set forms. He stands accused of starting the tale that Saint Denis the Areopagite's relics reached Ratisbon, and of forging exemption letters for his abbey. His Dialogue on his own trials marks the start of medieval autobiography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-angulo:
Pedro Angulo, a native of Burgos in Spain, came to America in 1524 as a soldier. He joined the Dominicans in 1529 and became a companion of Las Casas in Guatemala, Central America generally, and the greater Antilles. Made Dominican provincial for Chiapas and Bishop of Vera Paz, he died soon after, in 1561. He ranks among the earliest Indian missions' chief figures in southern Mexico and Guatemala, judged to outstrip Las Casas in importance, ability, and success.

His devotion to the work overcame every obstacle: he went from tribe to tribe, living and teaching among them. Seeing Indians grasp things more by eye than ear, he used charts where Bible subjects were shown allegorically. He carried them through wilderness as illustrations for his talks to natives. He mastered two Indian tongues, Nahuatl and Zutuhil, and wrote several religious tracts in the latter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-fullo:
Peter Fullo was a usurping Monophysite patriarch of Antioch who died in 488. His Greek surname, Gnapheus, came from his trade as a fuller of cloth, worked while he was a monk among the Sleepless Monks near Chalcedon. Expelled for loose living and heretical teaching, he won a priest's post through the future emperor Zeno, then stirred Antioch against Patriarch Martyrius and seized the see in 470.

His badge was a phrase added to the Trisagion, saying the Crucified One suffered for us in a sense that made Father and Spirit share the cross. The emperor deposed him in 471, he seized the see again in 476, was banished in 478, and was restored by the usurper Basiliscus in 485. He held Antioch until his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-capero:
Pietro Caperolo was a Franciscan preacher whose energy split a province of his order in the 1470s. He was a Friar Minor of unknown birth date, prized as a preacher at Brescia, Velletri, and other north Italian cities. He threw himself into the quarrel between the Franciscan provinces of Milan and Venice, sharpened by war between the two states.

With much effort he won Pope Sixtus IV's leave to detach several Venetian convents from the Observants. He formed a vicariate under the Conventuals that still chose its own superior. His followers were called Caperolani after him, but on his death at Velletri in 1480 the new branch dissolved, and every house returned to the Observants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pinerolo:
Pinerolo is a Piedmontese city and diocese in northern Italy, long a key fortress of the dukes of Savoy. It was first mentioned in the tenth century and ruled at first by its abbots. It passed under Savoyard protection in 1235 and full control in 1243, fell to France in 1536 and again in 1630, and returned to Savoy by the Treaty of Turin.

Its churches include a ninth-century cathedral with a fine bell tower and the Gothic San Maurizio, whose belfry looks out over the Alps. Founded as an abbey in 1064 by Adelaide of Susa and made a diocese in 1748, it counts fifty-eight parishes, and within its bounds stands the famous fortress of Fenestrelle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reyer-anslo:
Reyer Anslo, Dutch poet and convert, was born at Amsterdam in 1622 and died at Perugia in 1669. His parents were Mennonites, and he was baptized on 16 November 1646 and raised in that sect. Already famous as a poet, he earned his native city's laurel crown and silver dish for a poem honouring the new town hall. A poem honouring Sweden's Queen Christina, the Swedish Pallas, won him a golden chain.

In 1651 he entered the Catholic Church with forty-three others, as Jesuit manuscript records attest. In Rome he became secretary to Cardinal Capponi and received a gold medal from Pope Innocent the Tenth for his poetry. His works include a tragedy, The Parisian Blood-Bridal, on the Massacre of Saint Bartholomew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rodriguez-san:
Rodriguez Sanchez de Arevalo was a learned Spanish bishop and writer on church and state. Born in 1404 in the diocese of Segovia, he studied law at Salamanca for ten years and graduated as doctor. He served John II and Henry IV of Castile as secretary and envoy, opposing the Council of Basle's parliamentary theories at the Holy See.

After Calixtus III rose, he stayed at Rome and became Bishop of Oviedo. He later commanded the Castle of St Angelo under Paul II, who moved him in turn to Zamora, Calahorra, and Palencia. Printed works include the Speculum Vitae Humanae of 1468, on the lights and shadows of life's estates. They include the Historia Hispanica to 1469 and De Monarchia Orbis of 1521, asserting the pope's sole right to punish kings. His bold rebukes led Matthaeus Flaccus to call him a forerunner of Luther, quite unjustly, as Niccolo Antonio showed. He died in 1470.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saltillo:
Saltillo, a Mexican diocese suffragan of Linares, or Monterrey, covers the state of Coahuila, 63,728 square miles, with 357,652 people by the 1910 census. Its chief city, Saltillo, sits 5,190 feet above sea level and counted 35,063 people, serving as home to both bishop and state governor. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces a frontier see.

Founded in 1575 by Francisco de Urdinola, the city mixed Huachichil and Borrado Indians with Tlaxcalans brought by the Spanish, and Franciscan Andrés de León preached there in the sixteenth century. Renamed Ciudad Leona Vicario in 1827 for a Mexican heroine, it kept its old name in practice. Jalisco Franciscans held eight Coahuila missions under Linares until Leo XIII erected Saltillo as its own see in 1891.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-gallo:
San Gallo names a celebrated family of architects, sculptors, painters, and engravers who flourished in Renaissance Italy from the mid-fifteenth to the late sixteenth century. Founder Francesco Giamberti, a Florentine wood-carver who lived from 1405 to 1480, fathered Giuliano and Antonio. Their entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a dynasty of makers.

Giuliano da Sangallo, architect and sculptor from 1445 to 1516, trained under Francione, then went to Rome. Study of Vitruvius fired his love of antiquity there, and he worked on the Palace of San Marco for Cardinal Barbo, later Paul II. Back in Florence he shone as a military engineer, fortifying Ostia harbour in 1483 for Cardinal della Rovere, and spent his later years in Medici service and protection. The entry traces the family's buildings and fortunes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-francis-ca:
Francis Caracciolo, co-founder of the Minor Clerks Regular, found his vocation in a letter delivered to the wrong man. Baptized Ascanio in 1563 at Villa Santa Maria in the Abruzzi, he was cured of leprosy at twenty-two and vowed himself to church life, giving his goods to the poor. Studying theology at Naples, he was ordained in 1587 and joined the Bianchi della Giustizia, who helped condemned criminals die holy deaths. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Agnone to 4 June 1608.

A letter from Giovanni Agostino Adorno, seeking another Ascanio Caracciolo for a new institute, reached our saint by mistake in 1588. He read the error as God's will, helped draft the congregation's rules, and saw Sixtus V approve it on 1 July 1588. The entry turns a postal slip into a founding, and a leper's cure into a priest's career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gaspare-de:
Gaspare del Bufalo founded the Missionaries of the Most Precious Blood after a childhood cure he credited to Francis Xavier. Born at Rome on Epiphany 1786 to Antonio, chief cook of the Altieri princes, and Annunziata Quartieroni, he was confirmed at eighteen months for delicate health. An eye malady threatening blindness yielded to prayers to Xavier in 1787, and Gaspare kept the apostle as his congregation's patron. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 28 December 1837.

From childhood he showed horror even of venial sin, deep piety, mortification, mastery of a fierce temper and strong will, and heroic love for the poor. Entering the Collegium Romanum at twelve, he took first tonsure in 1800. The entry's early chapters show a Roman boy, frail of eye and strong of will, formed for a missionary order devoted to Christ's blood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-odilo:
Odilo, fifth abbot of Cluny, turned a single great monastery into the centre of a reforming network. Born about 962 to Auvergne nobility, he entered Cluny in 991 and became abbot before Mayeul's death in 994. Gentleness, charity, and a talent for organisation drove rapid growth under his rule.

He encouraged learning, set Radolphus Glaber to write a history of the age, and raised a magnificent monastery church. Monasteries under Cluny grew from thirty-seven to sixty-five, with five newly founded and twenty-three reformed. His reform reached Spain under Alfonso VI and prepared the union of houses that Hugo later completed. He died on 31 December 1048, famed for prayer and for All Souls' Day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-teilo:
Teilo, archbishop of Llandaff, shaped the Welsh Church from a monastic school that bore his name. Born at Eccluis Gunniau near Tenby, cousin of David, he was educated by Dyfrig at Hentland and by Paulinus at Whitland. He later ruled the monastic school at Llandaff, called Bangor Deilo after him.

The earliest lives are late and uncritical. A tale of his visit to Palestine with David and Padarn about 518, with consecration by John III of Jerusalem, is not now generally credited. His true name may have been Eliau, appearing in Latin as Teliarus and in Breton as Teliau. He died at Llandilo Vawr, probably in or before 560, an old man, though Ussher puts his death at 604.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-taos-pueblo:
Taos is an important Pueblo town on the Taos River in New Mexico. It lies about fifty miles northeast of Santa Fe. Its people speak Tigua, of Shoshonean stock. From some 2,500 people in 1630 and 2,000 before the revolt of 1680, it shrank to 578 in 1788. It stands now at about 450. Coronado's men first reached it in 1540. Franciscans founded San Geronimo de Taos about 1620.

In the great revolt of 1680, Taos served as headquarters of Pope, the rebellion's leader. Its two missionaries were killed. Missions revived after the reconquest some fifteen years later, then faded under Ute and Navaho raids. In 1847 townsfolk resisting American rule killed Governor Bent and others. American troops stormed the town, killing some 150 and executing sixteen more. The old feast of San Geronimo on 30 September still draws crowds for a relay race.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tiepolo:
Tiepolo covers two Venetian painters, father and son, in a single entry. Giovanni Battista Tiepolo was born at Venice in 1696, the son of a sea captain who left a good fortune. He married Cecilia Guardi in 1721 and fathered nine children. Studying Titian, Piazzetta, Ricci and above all Veronese, he became the last great Venetian painter.

He worked in Venice and northern Italy until 1750, spent three years painting ceilings at Wurzburg, and in 1761 went to Madrid at Charles III's invitation to decorate the royal palace. There the rivalry of Raphael Mengs embittered his last years, and he died at Madrid in 1770. His son Giovanni Domenico, born in 1727, assisted him but never matched his draughtsmanship or colour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trujillo:
A diocese in north-west Peru, comprising Lambayeque, Libertad, Piura and the province of Tumbes. Gregory XIII formed it on 13 April 1577 as a suffragan of Lima. Its city was founded in 1535 by Gonzalo Pizarro on the Río Muchi and named for his native place. It became the first Peruvian city to proclaim independence from Spain.

Most houses stand only one story high because of frequent earthquakes, the worst in 1619, 1759 and 1816. Near the city lie the ruins of Gran Chimu, or ChanChan, stretching twelve miles by six, with walls nine metres high and great burial mounds. From these ruins the Spaniards recovered over £5,500,000 in gold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-uccello:
Paolo Uccello was a Florentine painter born in 1397 who died in 1475. He is famed less for his given name than for his nickname, earned from his love of painting birds. His real name was Paolo di Dono. Apprenticed to Ghiberti, he helped prepare the first bronze doors for the Florence baptistery before setting up on his own. Geometry and perspective became his ruling passion, taught in part by the mathematician Manetti. Vasari mocked the devotion as wasted time.

Yet his skill in foreshortening and proportion was remarkable, and his battle scenes and frescoes show a painter wrestling with depth on a flat wall. The entry weighs Vasari's gibe that he grew more needy than famous against the view that his experiments opened ground later painters used. It lists his chief works and their churches, offering a compact life of an artist remembered for his obsession as much as his pictures.
dick-prescott-s-second-year-at-west-poin:
Year two at West Point fills H. Irving Hancock's second Dick Prescott book, on finding the glory of the soldier's life. Twenty-four chapters open with the class president lecturing on hazing. Plebe Briggs learns a few things, and Greg debates between girls and mischief.

Dick stands under a fearful charge, in close arrest, and on trial by court-martial. Friends stand by, and a verdict and a hop follow. A new cadet corporal is named in orders in the sampled middle, with Mr Dodge taking the place of a busted Ryder. Prescott, it is said, would have had the post but for his name for dodging scrapes. Barracks fights, the riding drill, and baseball fill the rest of the year.
doe-osti-17171715-hawc-multi-messenger-a:
Joshua Litchfield, a SULI intern at Los Alamos mentored by Kelly Malone, built an alert system linking the HAWC gamma ray observatory with other detectors, in a report dated August 2026. Multi messenger astrophysics gains when one observatory's event is checked against another's in near real time. HAWC watches the sky for very high energy gamma rays from a mountain site.

Methods define a HAWC alert metric, then run a coincident event search with the IceCube neutrino observatory, looking for events that line up in time and direction. A likelihood study of the source LHAASO J2108+5157 tests the machinery on a known object. The system aims to flag joint events fast enough for follow up telescopes to catch fading sources.
doe-osti-2572976-bringing-inorganic-carb:
DOE Basic Energy Sciences final report DE-SC0018020, by Hannah S. Shafaat of Ohio State University and dated July 24, 2025, closes a project that ran from September 2017 to August 2023. Nature's CODH/ACS enzyme pair turns carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide and then into acetyl-CoA, a basic fuel of life. The chemistry is industrially tempting, but the enzymes are huge, fragile, and oxygen-sensitive, so their mechanisms stay murky.

Shafaat's group built small, sturdy stand-ins instead. Two small proteins, ferredoxin and azurin, were reworked to host versions of the enzyme active sites, including the unusual four-iron, four-sulfur, nickel cluster. One line of work aimed at an artificial carbon monoxide dehydrogenase in a semisynthetic construct. The other probed the synthase side. Studying the mimics was meant to reveal metal oxidation states, binding sites, and intermediate structures that the native system hides.
doe-osti-2575368-em-shaping-symmetry-and:
Final technical report DE-SC0022229, led by Gregory M. Grason of UMass Amherst with E. Bryan Coughlin and Edwin L. Thomas of Texas A&M, covers September 2021 to February 2025. Block copolymers self-assemble into triply-periodic networks, sponge-like nanostructures prized for photonics, supercapacitors, and filtration membranes. Almost all work had stuck at one symmetry, the cubic double gyroid, because nobody could predict how chain packing shapes the rest.

The project established a medial packing paradigm for these assemblies. Its measure, medial thickness, reads how far each polymer block stretches from the dividing surface into the domain's middle, a direct gauge of packing frustration. Slice-and-view electron microscopy rebuilt real domains in three dimensions so the measure could be checked against experiment. Field theory calculations confirmed that chains tend to follow the medial map. Twelve papers and two dissertations came out of the award.
doe-osti-2585494-water-cooled-helmholtz-:
Gabriel Wiser's report, SAND2025-09674R, presents the design of a water-cooled Helmholtz coil for ultra-low magnetic field testing. Precise work with very small fields suffers when stray fields and trapped flux in superconducting magnets shift the field a test object actually feels. The coil was designed to wrap around a helium-3 cryogenic fridge with a 17.825-inch outer diameter, both to zero out stray fields and to sharpen field sweeps.

Wiser supports the design with finite volume modeling and finite element analysis. The models show the coil can run at 20 amperes indefinitely, producing a field of 65 millitesla. At that load the surface facing the fridge stays below 50 degrees Celsius. The report also does the practical math of ownership: the full parts list comes to 4,882.76 dollars.
doe-osti-2588880-structural-uncertainty-:
Stefan Domino of Sandia National Laboratories wrote this report, SAND2025-11249, printed September 2025, on structural uncertainty in large eddy simulation. The question is not whether a turbulence model is wrong, all subgrid models are approximations, but how much the choice among respectable models moves the answer. Two canonical flows serve as the test beds: plane channel flow and the periodic hill.

Three subgrid models are compared in wall-resolved, low-Mach simulations: WALE, a standard k-equation model, and the Inagaki k-equation variant. Implementation details come first, then each flow is computed with each model. One clear finding concerns near-wall behavior. The static coefficient k-equation model shows non-standard asymptotic behavior near the wall, a first-order dependence on wall distance where theory expects otherwise. The low-Reynolds corrected Inagaki form behaves differently. Results like these show users which parts of a prediction are model choice, not physics.
doe-osti-2589495-methodology-for-determi:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory final report NREL/TP-2800-96453 closes cooperative project CRD-21-21474 on lab methods for corn ethanol plants. Technical contacts Katie Michel and Justin Sluiter led work to measure the fiber part of corn kernels more completely. Plants earn credit under the Renewable Fuel Standard for the share of kernel fiber converted to fuel, so the measurement matters.

The method targets total cellulosic glucan, counting both cellulose and beta-glucans, plus hemicellulose, the other main fiber sugars. One task checked how much glucan is lost when samples pass through a cold caustic extraction step. Nuclear magnetic resonance runs on standard reference biomass confirmed starch signals that can confuse results. The outcome is one shared procedure the dry-grind ethanol industry can apply the same way at every plant.
doe-osti-3011000-preliminary-assessment-:
Low temperature chlorination of aluminium clad used nuclear fuel is assessed in SRNL-STI-2025-00645 by Vinh Nguyen and Thomas Shehee of Savannah River National Laboratory. Recent work with disulfur dichloride and thionyl chloride is summarised as groundwork for separating uranium from cladding and alloying elements. The assessment identifies two development needs, reaction kinetics and reagent quality.

A Uruguay fuel plate held at the laboratory, a U-Alx fuel meat with low enriched uranium and about 0.08 percent burnup, is analysed as a candidate for bench scale chlorination tests. Proposed next steps cover kinetic studies, reagent quality checks, and machining the plate to a suitable size before testing.
doe-osti-3011944-laboratory-investigatio:
Aerosol cloud interactions under entrainment are measured in a cloud chamber for the final report on award DE-SC0022128. Will Cantrell and Raymond Shaw of Michigan Tech led the work, with Fan Yang of Brookhaven National Laboratory. The Pi Chamber experiments are the first lab entrainment studies since Latham and Reed in 1977. Large eddy runs with the System for Atmospheric Modeling round out the measurements.

Droplet size response to mixing proved locally inhomogeneous yet globally homogeneous. The system rests in multiple equilibrium states, which explains the two readings. Simulations showed inhomogeneous marks for single mixing events but homogeneous pattern across an ensemble. Polluted clouds showed stronger inhomogeneous mixing in the model.
doe-osti-3015674-fundamentals-of-solar-p:
Why solar mounting bolts work loose is explained in a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report dated January 2026, by Jon Ness of Matrix Engineering Consultants and Gerald Robinson. Loose joints let modules shift, wear, and fail, and the report splits loosening into two families: rotation under vibration, and relaxation, where preload fades without the nut turning.

Relaxation mechanisms get the deep treatment: yielding of joint parts, fretting wear, surface embedment, and differential thermal expansion. Fixes follow the physics, including longer bolt grip lengths, Belleville springs, fewer joint interfaces, and washers sized to spread bearing stress. Retightening works but is often impractical across a solar field, which pushes design toward joints that hold preload from the start. A SETO failure survey grounds the mechanisms in field reports.
doe-osti-3023375-energy-cost-estimate-to:
Andrew Speake and Noel Merket of the National Laboratory of the Rockies document the Energy Cost Estimate Tool, version 2.0, in report NLR/TP-5500-95621, dated March 2026. The tool predicts home energy use and cost, and this volume explains the method behind it plus how to use it. Predictions lean on modeled building data rather than meter readings from each house.

Models were trained and checked with cross-validation, so test buildings were never seen during training. Median predictions are expected to be the most accurate and can be compared directly against the test dataset, unlike the other quartile regression models. Scatterplots compare ResStock modeled test data with median predicted energy use by fuel type across all building types, letting readers judge where the estimates run high or low.
doe-osti-3030033-resstock-measure-docume:
Sinoun Phoung, Yingli Lou, and Philip White of the National Laboratory of the Rockies document an attic upgrade in report NLR/TP-5500-96739, dated April 2026. The note is part of the ResStock series, which models retrofit choices across the United States housing stock. This measure adds insulation to the floor of an unfinished attic, the layer that separates heated rooms below from cold roof space above. The write-up gives the upgrade method and a brief look at key results.

Inside the model, home traits are turned into simulation inputs through lookup tables. The attic measure is coded as a change to the ceiling insulation value of each sampled home. The note lists the argument values the upgrade passes to the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow and points readers to the baseline stock papers for calibration and validation detail.
doe-osti-3031073-power-management-soluti:
Jesse Bennett, Gustavo Campos, Mohammad Bani Shamseh, and colleagues at the National Laboratory of the Rockies tackle airport power growth in report NLR/TP-5400-98768, dated April 2026. Airport rental car sites are adding fleets of electric cars, and their charging load could outgrow the local grid. The Athena team plan pairs flexible loads with on-site generation and storage. Shifting when cars charge can shave coincident peaks, delay costly grid upgrades, and cut power bills.

Bench work mapped charger efficiency across its full range. At low output the tested unit ran near 80 percent efficiency, peaked near 97 percent at 8 kilowatts, and settled near 90 percent for most of the cycle. High-use tests with Delta hardware added vehicle-side losses, so planners can size the system on real numbers.
doe-osti-3377326-adapting-high-resolutio:
A Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory project, led by Daniel J. Den Hartog, adapts X-ray microcalorimeter spectrometers for magnetic fusion plasma work. Den Hartog holds the grant at Livermore; the University of Wisconsin-Madison is funded apart. Microcalorimeters read X-ray photons with energy detail. The team installed and ran a system on the Madison Symmetric Torus. It pairs the spectra of crystal instruments with the reach of pulse-height systems.

Fusion devices need impurity data that older tools give slowly or coarsely. The diagnostic promises absolute measures of impurity ion build-up in the core plasma. It also reads the impurity ion temperature. Gains sought next are sharper spectra, wider coverage, and faster time steps. Small port access is a core design need. The hosted text's lettering is encoding-shifted, so fine detail beyond its main lines is hard to check.
doe-osti-3377654-risk-management-for-oce:
David Snowberg of the National Laboratory of the Rockies gives a training deck, dated May 7, 2026, on risk management for ocean-based technologies. The training rests on the laboratory's Marine Energy Technology Development Risk Management Framework, published in 2024 to replace the 2015 version. It links users to a Risk Register template and an FMECA worksheet, and it reproduces parts of IEC standards with permission.

The slides walk through why risk management matters for devices that must survive at sea, then move into risk identification step by step. One section treats policy risk, using the VUCA lens of volatility, uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity, with examples such as rules changing abruptly after an election. Marine energy methods carry over to other ocean technologies with the changes the deck flags.
doe-osti-3382891-best-practices-for-resi:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL-26/26, dated February 2026, gives best practices for developing and managing resilience hubs in East St. Louis, Illinois. The authors are Lawrence Paul Lewis and Susan Jones of Argonne, Drazenka Svedruzic of the National Laboratory of the Rockies, and Sophie Thuis of the Carbon League. The League and its community partners have identified five facilities to serve as hubs.

A hub supports its neighborhood in three modes. They are blue-sky everyday service, gray-sky preparation before an event, and black-sky emergency response. The memo lays out a roadmap of operations improvements and program planning. It gives advice on facility services, safety and physical protection, and community services. Operating protocols are covered too. A phased rollout plan is aligned to realistic funding and capacity limits, so a hub opens only when the money and staff are there.
doe-osti-3384959-gorman-a-framework-for-:
GORMan: A Framework for Governance, Ontologies, and Risk Management of Scalable Cross-Sector Integration of Secure Energy-Water Infrastructure Information, Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4409, is dated January 2026. Hillary K. Fishler, Alex B. May, and Katie Knight of Oak Ridge wrote it with Narcisa Pricope of Mississippi State University and Luc Rebillout of the University of Mississippi.

Energy and water systems lean on each other's data, but the data lives in separate sectors with separate rules. GORMan proposes the connective framework: governance for who may share what, ontologies so the systems describe the same things in the same terms, and risk management for the exposure that sharing creates. The author team's home divisions, critical infrastructure resilience and research computing, match the framework's two halves, infrastructure and information.
doe-osti-3403177-affordable-large-scale-:
Report ORNL/TM-2026/4686 from Oak Ridge National Laboratory, dated June 2026, covers a CRADA with re:3D Inc. to build a low-cost, large granulator. Peter Wang, Cait Clarkson, Shramana Ghosh, and co-authors report the work. The machine turns reclaimed plastic into feed for large printers.

The full line has four steps: grind whole water bottles, sort the flakes by plastic type, remove water, then dry the flakes. Dried granulate feeds the GigabotX printer named in the text. Each step was designed, built, tested, and revised in turn. The goal is cheaper recycled feedstock for firms that print big parts.
doe-osti-3579363-development-of-a-framew:
Argonne report ANL-AMMT-030 sets out a first framework for a design guide on environmental effects in advanced reactor materials. Bipul Barua of Argonne wrote it with Heramb P. Mahajan and Rongjie Song of Idaho and Caleb P. Massey of Oak Ridge. Parts in these reactors face high heat, repeated loading, neutron damage, and coolant contact. Current ASME rules for hot service do not yet cover those environmental effects directly.

The guide treats neutron damage as an added layer on the current design process. With sparse data, it applies two cut factors, one on creep-rupture strength and one on fatigue life. With fuller data, it traces each material property through four design checks. Sample values worked from a compiled set of annealed Type 316 steel data show how the math runs. Coolant effects are left for later work.
doe-osti-3827013-commercial-microgrid-or:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2026/4808, dated August 2026, builds a commercial orchestrator for networked microgrids. Guodong Liu and Maximiliano Ferrari of Oak Ridge wrote it with Jonanthan Lee of New Sun Road. Single microgrids often sit unbalanced, with too much solar at noon and too little at dusk. Linking several grids lets them trade power and smooth those swings. Oak Ridge designed the negotiation method; New Sun Road folded it into its Stellar platform, which runs many grids today.

The orchestrator settles trades through a step-by-step scheme that needs no central boss. Two new services join the platform inside its cloud host. Operator screens show grid groups and trade activity. Guard rules cover data safety and safe links between grids. The report flags attack paths through partner grids as open research, outside this first build. Tests checked that the commercial build follows the lab design.
dry-farming-a-system-of-agriculture-for-:
John A. Widtsoe's Dry-Farming, published in New York in 1920 with a preface dated 1910, systematizes farming without irrigation. Widtsoe, president of the Agricultural College of Utah, opens with a striking measure. Nearly six tenths of the earth's land receives less than twenty inches of rain a year. Irrigation can reclaim only a fraction of that vast area.

The rest must be won, if at all, by dry-farming: storing soil moisture, fallowing, and choosing crops for thirst. Widtsoe assembles the science of his day, from soil physics to plant water needs. He writes for the actual farmer first and the investigator second. Hilgard of California and King of Wisconsin are named as princes of soil study. The book founded a discipline that the dry American West and other arid lands still practise.
george-eliot-a-critical-study-of-her-lif:
George Willis Cooke published this critical study of George Eliot in 1884, just a few years after her death. Eliot, the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, wrote Middlemarch, Adam Bede, and The Mill on the Floss. Cooke had already written a like study of Emerson. A preface to the second edition owns an error: an essay he quotes was in fact written by George Henry Lewes, Eliot's partner.

Cooke traces her youth, her work as a translator and editor, her union with Lewes, and the slow rise of her fame. He weighs her poems, her essays, and each novel, and sets out the philosophy of sympathy that runs through them. The book is an early, earnest try at a full account of a writer whose work still shapes the English novel.
mademoiselle-of-monte-carlo:
Mademoiselle of Monte Carlo is a mystery novel by William Le Queux, dated 1921. It opens at a roulette table known as the Suicide's Table. A young Englishman stares at a handsome woman who is winning heavily. He is sure he has seen her somewhere before.

Her face is tied to his poor father's mysterious end. If she would only tell what she knows, the mystery might clear. But her reputation warns that she will never speak. Le Queux fills the tale with casinos, secrets, and pursuit. The Riviera's glitter hides danger at every table. It is a brisk thriller of the old school.
messer-marco-polo:
Donn Byrne published this lyrical retelling of Marco Polo's travels in 1921. Byrne was an Irish-American storyteller raised in Ireland and educated in Dublin. The book made his reputation, as the editor's note explains. It opens with a hunting scene in Ireland, where the tale is framed.

From that frame, the story follows the Venetian traveler to the court of Kublai Khan. Byrne retells desert crossings, court splendors, and eastern wonders in poetic prose. He writes history as romance rather than as record. The book won him a large and devoted readership, and his public kept growing.
nasa-tm-19660021043-experiment-on-pendul:
Guenter R Riegler at Goddard ran an experiment in March 1966 on how a balloon gondola swings in flight. A gondola hangs below a great balloon on long lines. It can swing like a pendulum and can also slowly rotate. Instruments in the gondola need a steady platform to aim at stars or at the Sun. Unsteady aim blurs or ruins their readings.

Riegler's experiment measured the pendulum and rotational motion during real flight, per the catalog note. Knowing the swing's size and rhythm is the first step to damping it. Balloon astronomy was a cheap path above most of the air. Its value rose or fell with the steadiness of the platform, which this work set out to measure.
nasa-tm-19670009371-lightweight-battery-:
Truman H. Kaehler, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this report in October 1966. It presents a design method for lightweight battery containers on satellites, worked out for Explorer XVII, the atmospheric structure satellite. On a spacecraft, every extra pound of structure steals from the instruments, so even the battery box deserved a fresh look.

Kaehler's design uses the batteries themselves as structural members, so the container adds little dead weight. At the same time, the batteries stay easy to remove for recharging on the ground. Sections of the report cover the design, its fabrication, and testing and evaluation. Explorer XVII itself was a sealed stainless steel sphere, thirty-five inches across, measuring density, pressure, composition, and electron temperature in the upper atmosphere.
nasa-tm-19670009435-status-of-superpress:
E. D. Angulo, J. G. Guidotti, and C. E. Vest, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, surveyed an industry in this December 1966 report. Their subject is superpressure balloon technology in the United States. The survey was driven by the FR-2 program, a joint United States and France satellite project using constant-level balloons.

The authors found the technology lagging behind other space-age fields. Long-life superpressure balloons, they report, had not been flown with satisfactory reliability. Problems in design, fabrication, and testing had to be solved before large numbers could fly cheaply and well. They recommended a funded development and testing program.
nasa-tm-19670029746-rapid-neutron-captur:
J. W. Truran, W. D. Arnett, S. Tsuruta, and A. G. W. Cameron study how stars forge the elements in this paper. The authors worked at institutes in New York and Cambridge, Massachusetts. Their subject is rapid neutron capture in supernova explosions, the so-called r-process.

Recent studies of the cores of highly evolved massive stars set the stage. The authors consider what those core conditions mean for building new elements. The conditions estimated for the models look very promising, they find. In them, nuclei can capture neutrons on a fast time scale before decaying. That is exactly what the r-process needs to build heavy elements.
nasa-tm-19680027301-automated-ground-sta:
Automated Ground Station Software Development is a Goddard Space Flight Center report dated October 1967, numbered X-521-67-492. It lays out how software was built for a prototype automated ground station. The station stood at the Network Test and Training Facility, where Goddard's tracking and data teams developed it together. Its design goal was bold: one computer controlling four satellite tracking links at once.

Fifteen station functions were identified, spanning pass scheduling, equipment logs, inventory control, setup, and status checks. The work proceeded through systems analysis, system design, program development, coding, and testing. A fast computer with disc and tape storage sat at the center. The report preserves an early blueprint for running tracking stations by software.
othello: Othello is William Shakespeare's tragedy, one of the most famous plays in English. The hosted sample, though, contains none of its text. It shows an introductory note by Project Gutenberg founder Michael S. Hart. Hart explains the strange spellings in old editions. Printers packed type into blocks called cliches, ran short of letters, and swapped u for v. Many supposed errors are the printers', he argues, not Shakespeare's. This note therefore describes only the edition's presentation. The sample offers no passage of the play itself.
penn-trial-of-william-penn-founder-of-pe:
The Trial of William Penn records the proceedings at the Old Bailey in London in September 1670. Soldiers had seized the Quaker meeting house in Gracechurch Street on August 15, so Penn preached in the street nearby. He was arrested, and tried with William Mead before the Lord Mayor, Recorder, and aldermen on the first, third, fourth, and fifth of September.

The pamphlet prints the court, the charges, and the conduct of the trial, in which the jury's refusal to convict made legal history. This 1830 printing, priced at four pence, kept the case before the public. It remains a founding document of jury independence and religious liberty.
podcast-dannyjones-4sgGJywuXLo:
Max Zamilov, billed as a nuclear physicist, brings Danny Jones a proposed answer to one of the oldest engineering puzzles on earth: how the Egyptians built the Great Pyramid. His theory, he argues, explains the precision of the stones and the labor the standard account requires, and he presents it as a solved problem.

Jones walks the claim through the usual objections: the ramps, the workforce, the timeline. Zamilov answers from physics rather than archaeology, which is both the theory's novelty and its vulnerability. Egyptologists do not accept it, and the episode does not settle the matter. What it offers is a credentialed outsider's full case, laid out in conversation. Listeners can compare his numbers against the orthodox story and decide which strains belief less.
podcast-joerogan-IiXmNDYE6lo:
Joe Rogan turns his show to the NYPD's secret surveillance fund in a segment from the Joe Rogan Experience. The topic is a pool of money the New York police used to fund watch work away from plain view. Rogan hosts the segment.

Rogan works through how the fund was set up and what it paid for, as reports have shown. He asks how a police force in a free city can hold a secret purse for spying. The segment is short and sharp, built on one news tale. Listeners get a quick, hot take on a civic scandal. The library holds the file as an archive record.
statistical-historical-and-political-des: William Charles Wentworth wrote a Description of the Colony of New South Wales. Its full title adds the settlements in Van Diemen's Land. The book is at once statistical, historical, and political. Wentworth calls himself a native of the colony. G. and W. B. Whittaker printed the London book in 1819. The contents sort the work in four parts. A count of the settlements comes first. The working of the present system of rule follows. Changes in the colony's course and frame close the plan.
strange-visitors-a-series-of-original-pa:
Strange Visitors, dated 1871, bills itself as a series of original papers on philosophy, science, government, religion, poetry, art, fiction, satire, humor, narrative, and prophecy. Its title page says the pieces were dictated through a clairvoyant while in a trance state.

The supposed authors are the spirits of the famous dead: Irving, Thackeray, Bronte, Byron, Hawthorne, Wesley, Browning, and others now dwelling in the spirit world. The contents give Margaret Fuller on literature in spirit life. They give Byron answering his accusers. They give Napoleon addressing the French nation. Poe gets a piece called The Lost Soul. Artemus Ward reports from in and out of purgatory. It is a full specimen of American spiritualist publishing.
the-halo: Bettina von Hutten wrote The Halo, published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1907, with a frontispiece by B. Martin Justice. She is named as the author of Pam and Pam Decides, and the book is dedicated to the memory of a dear lost friend, dated at Thun, Switzerland, on September 5, 1907. Only the title pages, dedication, and the first lines of a prologue set on a dusty Norman road are present here.
the-queen-of-the-air-being-a-study-of-th:
John Ruskin lectures on Greek myths of cloud and storm, taking Athena as his central figure and recalling her help to Bellerophon in bridling Pegasus. The opening asks hearers to approach old faiths with patience and human sympathy rather than quick contempt.

Ruskin defines a myth as a story carrying a meaning beyond its surface, often marked by strange or unnatural details, and gives Hercules and the Lernaean serpent as an example. His point is that forgotten beliefs were once sincerely held. Readers interested in mythology, art, and Victorian thought find a humane method for reading ancient stories.
the-seven-little-sisters-who-live-on-the:
Jane Andrews wrote The Seven Little Sisters Who Live on the Round Ball That Floats in the Air. Louisa Parsons Hopkins, formerly a supervisor in Boston public schools, supplied an introduction. Andrews dedicated the stories to her three little friends, Marnie, Bell, and Geordie. The contents promise the ball itself, then sisters around the world. Agoonack the Esquimau sister and Gemila, child of the desert, appear. Pen-Se, a little dark girl, and Louise of the Rhine also figure.

Hopkins's memorial gives Andrews's dates as 1833 to 1887. She recalls a happy day when Andrews gathered friends in an old-fashioned parlor. Andrews read them the stories in this volume before offering them to a publisher. The parlor looked out on a broad, elm-shaded street. Hopkins offers her pages to show readers something of Andrews herself. Her way of writing and teaching is the subject.
tom-swift-and-his-undersea-search-or-the: The Treasure on the Floor of the Atlantic draws Tom Swift down in the undersea search story by Victor Appleton, presented through twenty-five chapter headings. Untold millions and a strange offer open the book. Later headings promise a sea monster, serpent weed, a devil fish, an undersea collision, and the treasure ship with its steel box. Chapter one begins with Tom calling some reading wonderful, mentioning over a hundred million, then stops. The contents and that fragment are what is present here.
un-doc-secretary-general-addressing-univ:
Students at a university in Beijing heard this appeal in 2004 from the Secretary-General of the United Nations. Speaking during a visit to China, he urged young people to commit themselves to the Millennium Development Goals. Those goals set shared targets on poverty, health, and schooling for 2015.

The address tells students that the goals belong to their generation most of all. It links China's rapid rise to a duty to help poorer states. It also praises youth service and study abroad. The speech shows how the UN chief of that era sold a global plan to a campus crowd.
